## Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Mr. Monk and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Mr. Monk Meets Alexander the Great" **·** Albert Camus, Diogenes the Cynic — The Myth of Sisyphus; The Absurd; Cynicism (living according to nature); Rebellion and Revolt — Wittkower argues that Monk's daily, unwinnable war on dirt and disorder is Camus's happy Sisyphus made concrete: Monk vacuums ceilings, touches lampposts, and solves murders knowing the dirt and the murderers will always return ('There's never hope... Hope. I hate hope's guts' in 'Mr. Monk Can't See a Thing'), yet he still finds enough satisfaction to take up the wipe again. Reading Ecclesiastes' vanity alongside the uncaring wasp of the opening, the chapter claims Monk shows us how to live wisely without resignation in an absurd world that does not care. He is paired with Diogenes the Cynic, whose barrel, raw onions, and midday lantern mirror Monk's pot-pie-Tuesdays and his refusal to overlook what everyone else ignores; like Diogenes telling Alexander the Great 'get out of my sun,' Monk lives by his own ideals no matter how society judges him. The essay closes that, like Camus addressing the Dominican monks, we should refuse to 'be reasonable' about evil and disorder and keep struggling without hope, wipe in hand.
- ch. 7 "I Just Solved the Case - How Monk Think" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "It’s a Gift ... and a Curse" **·** Edmund Husserl, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology — Welsh argues Monk's 'gift and curse' is being permanently stuck in Husserl's phenomenological attitude. Selective-attention experiments (the swapped interviewer behind the door, the gorilla-suit walker) show that the rest of us see only what expectation renders possible, while Monk, like Poe's Dupin finding the Purloined Letter in plain sight, brackets his assumptions and actually perceives: the moved decorative rock in Dr. Kroger's courtyard, the wing-back chair and wiped bullets proving the 'suicide' in 'Mr. Monk and the Garbage Strike' is murder, and the illiterate suspect's English-sign slip in 'Mr. Monk Goes to a Fashion Show' — all through his hand-framing 'Zen Sherlock Holmes thing.' But because he cannot exit back into the natural attitude, the same perception is pathological. Drawing on Damasio's Descartes' Error and Merleau-Ponty's patient Schneider, the chapter argues that emotion is what structures relevance and action, so Monk's refusal to let emotional bonds organize his life leaves him isolated and unhappy — though curing the curse might cost him the gift that solves the cases.
- ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" **·** Karl Popper, René Descartes — Falsificationism; The Best of All Possible Worlds; Ockham's Razor — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- ch. 10 "Step Back" **·** David Hume — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Problem of Induction — Gallagher uses Monk's phobias to test Hume's claim that believing is itself a kind of feeling. The chapter asks whether a fear conflicting with a rational belief (Monk paralyzed by the possibly-on stove during a murder investigation) feels any different from a conflict between two fears ('Snakes trump heights' in 'Mr. Monk and the Very, Very Old Man') or two beliefs, and answers with Hume that beliefs are forceful-feeling representations — there is a 'what it's like' to believing the German shepherd is dangerous. On Hume's account the force of a belief comes from repetition of experience, which explains both why Monk's fears should fade (countless safely landed flights, millions of milk drinkers) and why they persist: his mind dwells repeatedly on the rare catastrophe, giving fearful representations extra force, as when his repeated experience that 'she's always cheating' makes him wrongly believe Brody's wife in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully.' The practical lesson is to step back and widen attention to all the possibilities, as Monk intermittently manages with the help of Natalie and Stottlemeyer.
- ch. 11 "He’s the Guy - What Monk Is Made Of" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "You Don’t Have to Be Like Him to Like Him" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Golden Mean; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Levitt reads Monk through Aristotle's virtue ethics: a man of character whose police virtues survive Trudy's murder but whose phobias produce akrasia — in the pilot he knows he must descend the germ-filled sewer to save Sharona and freezes anyway, doing the right thing only at agonizing cost. Virtue as habit and the golden mean (friendliness as the mean between obsequiousness and standoffishness) frame his slow progress toward acting rightly without thinking, which is also why Stottlemeyer cannot recommend his reinstatement — he doubts the illness, not the man. Aristotle's three friendships sort Monk's relationships: utility (the department, employer Sharona), pleasure, and virtue — Natalie, who after watching Monk save Julie's fish over the priceless moon rock saw her late husband's goodness in him. Ethos, pathos, logos and catharsis then explain viewer identification: watching Monk move from akrasia toward balance (Dr. Kroger's 'N. Hope' note that turns out to mean New Hope) lets audiences identify with, and be ennobled by, a character we would never want to be.
- ch. 13 "It’s Time for the Other Walkie-Talkie" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Michel de Montaigne — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Philosophy of Love; Stoicism — Dodge puts Monk on the case of friendship's nature, structured by Aristotle's three kinds from the Nicomachean Ethics: Hal Tucker's fake buddy act in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend' is pure utility, while Natalie's is virtue-friendship — she is his friend 'in spite of' the job since 'he doesn't pay her that much.' The friend as mirror and 'second self' grounds the claim that Stottlemeyer, Sharona, Natalie and Randy reflect Monk's excellence back to him, and Bacon's point that a friend redoubles joys and cuts griefs in half is shown when they stay up all night during his suicide watch. Seneca's Stoic counsel — judge a person long before admitting him, then hold nothing back — is exemplified by Natalie's fish-over-moon-rock test of Monk's character, while Montaigne's once-in-centuries friendship in which two selves blur fits only Trudy, whose dying words 'bread and butter' tell Monk they belong together. Plato's Lysis (the 'great cosmic swirly' Monk cites in 'Mr. Monk and the Bully') opens the puzzle Socrates could not solve, and the single walkie-talkie his father gave him shows why the chapter's verdict — Monk now has friends — matters.
- ch. 14 "Mr. Monk’s Greatness" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Plato — The Übermensch; Existence Precedes Essence — Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').
- ch. 15 "Unless I’m Wrong, and I’m Not... - Monk’s Logic" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" **·** John Locke, David Hume, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Bundle Theory of Self — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- ch. 17 "Here’s How It Happened and Didn’t Happen" *(no index entry yet)* — Michaud asks how TV's most logical detective can assert contradictions: Monk says 'I know it's impossible, but he's the guy' about Derek Philby murdering while proctoring an exam ('Mr. Monk Goes Back to School') and about astronaut Steve Wagner killing while in orbit ('Mr. Monk and the Astronaut'), seeming violations of the Law of Non-Contradiction that his own valid arguments (the missing glass of water ruling out suicide) depend on. The chapter stages Graham Priest's dialetheism — the Liar Sentence as a true contradiction — as a possible defense, even borrowing Gricean maxims to argue Monk would announce a dialetheia if he believed one, but concludes Monk never actually accepts true contradictions: the impossible accusation creates a tension that drives him to find the hidden mechanism (Wagner's pre-rigged garage door), so the 'contradiction' dissolves once a false assumption is exposed. Michaud's closing suggestion is that the Liar Sentence itself should be treated as a crime to be solved rather than a dialetheia to be accepted.
- ch. 18 "Here’s What Happened" **·** The Myth of Sisyphus — Kane, a catalog librarian, argues that Monk's detecting mirrors library cataloging. Monk 'collocates' — identical boxes on one wall, a row of matching Trudy photos on another — and reasons user-first, exactly as Cutter's rule says to choose the entry a library's users will look under first: in 'Mr. Monk and the Bad Girlfriend' he sees the suspect with no alibi must be innocent because a killer who hides in the bathroom already has an alibi secured. Like the invisible cataloger, Monk imposes the order others see without knowing someone arranged it, and both face Sisyphus's rock: Monk's control ends at his apartment door ('Mr. Monk Makes the Playoffs' tailgate chaos), and Universal Bibliographic Control — one standard for describing every work ever created — will never stay at the top of the hill. The Cutter-versus-Dewey rivalry parallels Monk versus Harold Krenshaw, the flashy thunder-stealer who gets famous first, and the chapter ends by pronouncing Monk a natural-born cataloger.
- ch. 19 "He’s a Iteal Character - Monk Competition" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Identity" *(no index entry yet)* — Zaffran reads Monk and Dr. House as twin heirs of Sherlock Holmes — impossible crimes versus impossible diseases — both 'marked' like Oedipus, the first fictional detective, whose truth-seeking destroyed him: Monk's OCD begins with the unsolved murder of Trudy, which he feels implicated in, while House's limp, addiction and misanthropy trace to a misdiagnosis and childhood abuse. The chapter's core argument uses Bachelard's Prometheus complex, 'the Oedipus complex of intellectual life': both sleuths are punished for their insight, chained like Prometheus to their disorders (OCD; Vicodin and the bad leg), yet keep stealing the fire of explanation — their real goal is not justice or cure but disclosing the hidden how of each murder and disease. Monk and House are ultimately mirrors of their writers and audience: fiction (via Brian Boyd's evolutionary account) lets us rehearse moral situations and appease our fear of boredom, which is why we love these gift-and-curse characters and keep coming back for the next episode.
- ch. 21 "The Emotion-Reason Dilemma, Part II" **·** Michel Foucault — Feminism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Pribram places Monk and Dr. House in the tradition of the brilliantly rational but emotionally plagued detective (Dragnet's emotionless Joe Friday vs Cracker's Fitz), arguing both shows treat excessive emotion as the price of genius: Monk's OCD is tied to his pattern-spotting ('You're a freak of nature'), and when medication cures the OCD in 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' his detective genius vanishes. She applies Foucault's Birth of the Clinic to House's subtracting of the patient, but shows both series critique that modernist rationality through Eve in 'One Day, One Room', who forces House to face the rationally inexplicable. Using feminist scholarship (Jaggar, Alberti, Battersby), she argues the opposition of male reason to female emotion is a historically specific construction, and offers the best friends Stottlemeyer and Wilson as integrated alternatives who pay for their balance with ordinariness: polarization equals greatness, integration signals the mundane.
- ch. 22 "Herr Leibniz Consoles Mr. Monk" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, Ludwig Wittgenstein — The Best of All Possible Worlds; Principle of Sufficient Reason; Monadology — Kavas distinguishes Monk's method from Holmes's modus ponens, Poirot's elimination, and Goren's profiling: Monk accepts only what completes a coherent total narrative, so 'Here's what happened' re-tells the order of the whole world, as in the chess-game solution of 'Mr. Monk and the Genius'. The chapter uses the Tractatus's world of contingent, logically independent facts to model Monk's picture-completion, then brings in Leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason, the best of all possible worlds, and preestablished harmony justify Monk's faith that even Trudy's death must have a reason. Monk emerges as a pessimistic Leibniz who takes the world to be the worst possible precisely because, since learning the bomb was meant for Trudy in 'Mr. Monk Goes to Jail', he cannot see any sufficient reason for her death ('Why her?').
- ch. 23 "He’s ... Not Like Everyone Else - The Spiritual Side of Adrian Monk" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Does the Habit Make the Monk" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Anselm of Canterbury, Aristotle — The Ontological Argument; The Five Ways — Elliott maps the recurring Monk stalemate onto medieval theology: in 'Mr. Monk Goes to the Circus', Stottlemeyer and Disher reason forward from a hunch and the evidence, exactly like Anselm's ontological argument, which assumes what it sets out to prove, while Monk, like Aquinas against Anselm, refuses assumptions and reasons backward from verifiable facts, asking why an assassin would somersault except to advertise the acrobatic alibi. Aquinas's First Cause argument (Aristotle's unmoved mover) supplies the model of proving a certainty from observable things, paralleling Monk's 'I don't know how he did it, but he did it' backward deduction. The chapter's closing move likens Monk to the medieval monks themselves: his OCD-driven ascetic withdrawal from the dirty, chaotic world (contemptus mundi) is what lets him notice the imperfection in scenes like the locker room of 'Mr. Monk and the Big Game' that reveals sabotage.
- ch. 25 "Shaman, Heal Thyself" *(no index entry yet)* — Culver reads Monk as a shamanic figure in Arnold van Gennep's and Victor Turner's sense: a liminal man, neither cop nor civilian, fixed in the transitional stage of mourning Trudy, who heals society's disorder from its margins as Holmes and Poirot did. Drawing on Mary Douglas's Purity and Danger (dirt as defilement and disorder), she interprets Monk's ritualized gestures and utterances, framing the scene with his hands, the rare solving-smile, 'he's the guy' and 'Here's what happened', as the ceremonial performance by which disorder is overcome. Episodes like 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' and 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' then show the shaman's bind: whenever Monk attains purity or happiness he loses his sacred gift, so he must refuse to heal himself and remain 'a blessing and a curse'.
- ch. 26 "Mr. Monk Murdered Trudy" **·** The Buddha — Compassion (karuna); Emptiness (sunyata); Non-Self (anatman) — Green argues Monk is an unintentional Bodhisattva whose OCD enacts the Four Bodhisattva Vows: the compulsion to touch lampposts is the first vow's blind desires, his monastic minimalism the Dharma gate, and his crime-solving compassion for a disordered world the third vow, with the Dhammapada's teaching that the untamed mind produces suffering exemplified by Monk and by Harold Krenshaw's rival ordering. Like Vimalakirti feigning illness, or Shawn Spencer in Psych, and like the father in the Lotus Sutra's burning-house parable, Monk and his writers use skillful deception to awaken viewers to suffering and loving kindness. The title thesis is that Monk cannot solve Trudy's murder because he accepts responsibility for it: by Thich Nhat Hanh's Interbeing there is no absolute self and other, so solving the case requires the Zen 'kill the Buddha' eradication of the self, Monk's nirvana-as-extinction and the end of the series.
- ch. 27 "Our Hour Isn’t Over Yet, It’s Only Been Fifty-Eight Minutes - Monk in Therapy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "16 - Mr. Mead Starts Couples Therapy" *(no index entry yet)* — Clinical psychologist Sylvia Randall writes a thinly fictionalized case study in which 'Andrew Mead' (Monk: wife Terry killed violently, severe OCD, assistants Sheila/Sharona and Naomi/Natalie) brings his working relationships to couples therapy. Through 'I statements' and gentle confrontation, the sessions surface unconscious associations: Mead's fear that his father left because of him, his mother's OCD, Sheila's 'suck it up' childhood, and his survivor's guilt over joy since Terry's death, which an imagined conversation with Terry releases. The chapter's argument is the psychodynamic one that making unconscious material conscious lowers its emotional charge, widening the client's behavioral repertoire and restoring empathy and intimacy in the couple.
- ch. 29 "Mr. Monk, Jungle Guide" **·** Aristotle, The Buddha — Kagan reads Monk through Ernest Becker's Denial of Death: everyone is born hyper-aware like Monk and learns 'how not to see', managing the terror of the jungle out there through denial, shopping, and hero systems, which is why Randy Disher can ride in a cab driven by a corpse without noticing. Monk, who cannot forget (his nudity phobia traced to the trauma of his own birth in 'Mr. Monk and the Naked Man'), is our funhouse mirror and, like the Buddha seeing the four sights of sickness, old age, death, and the renunciant, he re-enters the world after Trudy's death to guide us through it. Aristotle's catharsis explains the pleasure of watching: pity and fear are burned off as Monk, more afraid than we are, still pursues truth and justice.
- ch. 30 "The Strength to Mourn" **·** Jacques Derrida — Tarantino and Wittkower read Monk through Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle: repetition compulsion (the fort/da child, the anxiety dream of running toward Trudy's car in 'Mr. Monk Is on the Run, Part 1') is the mind's attempt to retroactively prepare for trauma, which explains both the nudity phobia traced to Monk's birth and his endless return to Trudy's case. Monk's compulsions are also displacement behavior, standing in for the one disorder he cannot put in order, Trudy's death itself, which resists mourning because the beloved object cannot be de-cathected, a Derridean impossible mourning that leaves him haunted. Only when solving the crime proves empty does Monk reach the chapter's conclusion: happiness lies not in possessing lost objects of desire but in new emotional investment in a changing, uncertain world, which the authors name hope.
- ch. 31 "Case Files" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "I Organized Everything by Topic Alphabetically. You’ll Thank Me Later" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "Mr. Monk and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!

- ch. 1 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors introduce the volume by reading Gaiman's fiction as travel literature: heroes like Richard Mayhew in Neverwhere, Coraline, and Shadow in American Gods are forced or seduced into enchanted worlds that press against the mundane, and must map and decode those worlds to survive, transforming themselves in the process. They contrast tourists, who stay detached behind camera and guidebook, with travelers, who engage and are changed, and argue that reading Gaiman philosophically turns readers into travelers. They close with Gaiman's Newbery speech about stories as 'good lies that say true things' that leave readers changed forever.
- ch. 8 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Seneca — Philosophical Skepticism; Free Will vs Determinism — Elizabeth Swanstrom reads Mr. Wednesday's recruitment of Shadow in American Gods as a two-man con that exploits Hume's account of causation: because the mind projects causal links from constant conjunction, Odin and Loki stage a chain of 'coincidences' (Laura's death, rerouted flights, the first-class seat) and use classic misdirection, from Sweeney's warning at Jack's Crocodile Bar to the Herodotus tale of Croesus, so that the mark never looks at the hand with the coin in it. Setting Hume's billiard-ball analysis against Seneca and the Stoic idea of derivative causality, she argues Wednesday manipulates association rather than chance itself. Shadow's counter-training in coin sleights, especially the Sucker Vanish, and Sweeney's gift of the resurrection coin that revives Laura introduce genuine chance, letting Shadow see the set-up, stop the sacrificial battle, and demonstrate that a causally saturated world still leaves room to break the game.
- ch. 10 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Tripartite Soul; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Greg Littmann stages Plato's hypothetical review of American Gods under the Republic's charges against poetry: the novel is full of 'greatest of all lies' about gods behaving badly, from Odin and Loki's sacrificial plot to Czernobog's head-smashing, gods degrading themselves into lesser forms like Horus the road-kill-eating hawk and Media as Lucille Ball, and characters ruled by passion rather than reason, from Mad Sweeney drinking himself to death to Thor's suicide, corrupting a soul that should be governed by rationality. Against this he sets Aristotle's Poetics: listening to music and intellectual leisure are valuable in themselves, fiction is more philosophic than history because it shows what could happen, the impossible is justified when it astounds, and catharsis through pity for figures like the weeping Mad Sweeney purges rather than corrupts. Because American Gods' absurd premise unfolds with internally probable, character-consistent events (loyal Shadow, loving Laura, grifter Odin), it satisfies Aristotle's requirement that fantasy make artistic sense.
- ch. 11 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** John Dewey — Pragmatism; Truth as What Works — Ray Bossert reads American Gods as an allegory of American philosophy: like Gaiman's gods, American philosophers labor invisibly in the background while European publics canonize their thinkers, and Shadow's prison exchanges show the point, since Loki must beg him to read Herodotus ('It's cool') while Johnnie Larch's 'don't piss off people who work in airports' beats Shadow's abstract generalization in usefulness. Following Hickman's Deweyan instrumentalism, he argues the gods are survival tools humans craft from need and discard when obsolete, so Czernobog's hammer gives way to Media's television, Wednesday treats even his own son as an instrument, and the buffalo man's 'believe everything' is advice about keeping one's tools of survival working. The chapter ends on liberty: Shadow refuses to be a god because 'we don't need anyone to believe in us,' and in the Egyptian death trial he claims the most American reward, the freedom to choose his own afterlife.
- ch. 12 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Gottfried Leibniz, David Chalmers, René Descartes — Theory of Forms; Monadology; The Hard Problem of Consciousness; Allegory of the Cave — Richard Rosenbaum asks how Gaiman's gods, abstract concepts made flesh who live or die by human belief, could exist, starting from Plato's Forms (Odin as personified battle-wisdom, Media as media) and the Allegory of the Cave, which gives new meaning to a protagonist literally named Shadow. Finding Forms too independent to need believers, he upgrades the metaphysics with Leibniz's Monadology: if everything, bodies and ideas alike, is composed of perception-bearing monads, then shared beliefs can agglomerate, 'level up' into a soul, and become a living god walking around America. Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, panprotopsychism, and the claim that information has interdependent physical and phenomenal aspects supply the final mechanism, so collective belief realized phenomenally must become physically embodied, in contrast to the dualism of Descartes that made mind-body interaction mysterious.
- ch. 13 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, George Berkeley, Zhuangzi, Bertrand Russell, David Chalmers — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream); Philosophical Zombies — T. Bradley Richards takes The Sandman's Dreamworld seriously as a hypothesis: could our nightly dreams be travels to a mind-independent place like Morpheus's realm? Starting from Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Descartes's dream argument, he uses Berkeley's God-sustained idealism as a model for how Morpheus's mind could uphold the Dreamworld's order, and a thought experiment about glitchy dream-travel defuses Descartes's appeal to the discontinuity of dreams. Against the objection that dreams are blatantly contradictory ('it was Dave, but it also wasn't Dave'), he deploys Russell's theory of descriptions against Meinongian subsistence, Chalmers-style conceivability-implies-possibility reasoning from philosophical zombies, and Graham Priest's dialetheism, concluding that dreams could be experiences of an objective world, with waking and dreaming on a par.
- ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Hannah Arendt, Richard Rorty — The Banality of Evil; The Ethics of Care; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- ch. 16 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); The Cogito — Kandace Lytle maps Coraline's other mother onto Descartes's evil genius: a world-manipulating deceiver whose seductive sensory pleasures, from the gravy-train dinner to the adoring other father's songs, must be doubted in favor of the intellect, exactly as the wax argument shows that understanding comes from the mind and not the senses. Because Coraline enters the portal awake, Gaiman sidesteps the dream-skepticism worry and makes the other mother's world a parallel reality built to entrance, seduce, and possess her. Coraline's refusal to sew buttons in place of her eyes protects her autonomy and free will, the ghost children who lost their names and memories show what surrender costs, and the nameless cat's 'we know who we are, so we don't need names' guides her to the cogito, so that she defeats the deceiver by finding the 'I' in Coraline, a self-sufficiency the 2009 film version, the author argues, fails to capture.
- ch. 17 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Frank Jackson, Thomas Nagel — The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room); What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Being-Toward-Death — Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.
- ch. 19 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — The End of Grand Narratives — Wade Newhouse reads The Graveyard Book as a fusion of the coming-of-age tale and the Gothic ghost story, from The Turn of the Screw to Stephen King's haunted narcissists, and uses Lyotard's postmodern condition to explain the hybrid: Bod's self forms not by accepting one governing metanarrative but at Lyotardian 'nodal points' among many ghosts, each a fragment of history with its own partial morality, from the Roman Caius Pompeius to the witch Liza Hempstock. The Danse Macabre, where living and dead mix under rules neither remembers choosing, dramatizes borders that feel absolute, yet Bod's development consists in violating boundaries, befriending the outcast witch and hunting the Jacks on his own terms. The ending, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' offers a postmodern self most itself by being no one, with the acceptance of death as the one metanarrative even postmoderns keep, for Bod it is the first lesson rather than the last.
- ch. 20 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Najwa Al-Tabaa reads Sandman: Season of Mists through Derrida's paradox that only the unforgivable can truly be forgiven: Morpheus's freeing of Nada works as forgiveness precisely because condemning his lover to Hell was unforgivable, while Lucifer, who was never wronged by the damned, can give them only a devalued semblance of pardon, and they cling to punishment they feel they deserve. She then brings in Foucault's Discipline and Punish and Bentham's Panopticon to read the angels' rebuilt Hell of redemption as the modern rehabilitative prison, where watched souls are expected to reform themselves. The experiment fails, she argues, because redemption is imposed without hearing the prisoners, violating Derrida's condition that forgiveness needs a shared language, so the inmates prefer Lucifer's honest eternity of despair to a salvation they never asked for, a lesson about real prisons that seek rehabilitation through punishment.
- ch. 21 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Authenticity; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Wayne Yuen uses The Graveyard Book to teach the good life: Bod's family's murder, like students owing their existence to the Holocaust, is an unalloyed moral evil that still enables a better life, and Saul Smilansky's distinction between being 'sorry for' and 'sorry that' lets Bod benefit without endorsing the tragedy. His graveyard education is Aristotelian, virtues acquired through practice and models, from the Owenses' duty and Silas's wisdom to 'righteous indignation' against school bullies and friendship with Scarlett as intrinsically valuable, all building toward eudaimonia. The existentialist virtue of authenticity (attributed to Sartre and Kierkegaard) explains why Bod must be 'nobody but himself' rather than a copy of the vampire Silas, why the scavenged identities of the ghouls mark inauthenticity, and why wiping Scarlett's memory threatens her authenticity, resolving the apparent conflict between virtue and being oneself because bravery or wisdom is relative to the individual.
- ch. 22 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The Übermensch; The Death of God — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- ch. 24 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Bertrand Russell, Plato — Language Games — Tuomas Manninen asks how Gaiman's recycled mythological figures can be the same characters as their originals when Revelation's male, sword-wielding War becomes Good Omens' arms-dealing Carmine 'Red' Zuigiber and Pestilence retires in 1936 for Pollution, with the problem of talking truthfully about non-existent entities reaching back to Plato's Sophist. David Lewis's 'Truth in Fiction' makes the original author the arbiter of a character's properties, and Amie Thomasson's artifact theory makes fictional characters abstract artifacts created by authors, but only adding the type/token distinction and Wittgenstein's family resemblances, the same criss-crossing network of overlapping similarities by which we count games, lets Revelation's Four Horsemen and Gaiman's Four Bikers be tokens of one type. He closes with Russell's defense of philosophy's value: like Richard Mayhew's tale of London Below, a philosophical answer need not convince or be final to teach us 'what things may be.'
- ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Michel Foucault — Existence Precedes Essence; Authenticity; Bad Faith; Anxiety (the dizziness of freedom) — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.' Heidegger supplies the uncanny not-at-home-ness (unheimlich) of the graveyard, which Tally, citing Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' calls a heterotopia, while Silas the vampire embodies Lukacs's transcendental homelessness and Kierkegaardian anxiety is transmuted by Bod into the spectral gift of Fear he wields on his bullies. The identity-leeching ghouls named after the Duke of Westminster and the 33rd President are the avatars of bad faith, and the Jacks' attempt to dodge the prophecy fulfills it like Oedipus's, showing that Bod's fate, too, is self-made.

## Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield

- ch. 1 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The volume's introduction, 'Learning from the Insiders.' It introduces Orange Is the New Black (Piper Kerman's book and the Netflix series about Piper's time in Litchfield) and previews each contributor's topic: other minds, manipulation, the Prisoner's Dilemma, religion, existentialism, race, Crazy Eyes as Don Quixote, prisoners' moral obligations, Nietzsche on a trans woman, Aristotle on friendship, Bentham's panopticon, and Foucault on punishment. It frames the show as ripe for philosophy on punishment, moral obligation, existential themes, and race, gender, identity, and sexuality without itself applying any single theory.
- ch. 10 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Ludwig Wittgenstein — Bad Faith; Authenticity — Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.
- ch. 12 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Philosophy of Love — Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.
- ch. 13 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch — DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.
- ch. 15 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Carveth examines African-American portrayal on the show through Piper, Taystee, and Sophia: Piper's whiteness wins Healy's favoritism and makes her complicit in keeping the inmates powerless ('we understand each other, don't we?'), while Taystee's parole violation shows Litchfield as the only place she fits. Using Lippmann's account of media stereotypes, he credits the show with multidimensional characters of color but faults it for a 'white voice': Black women's incarceration is framed as bad choices and culture of poverty, and only Piper's SHU suffering is shown while Black and Latina women cycle through it. The series critiques the prison system yet stops short of showing the structural forces that leave its inmates no options.
- ch. 16 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; The Panopticon (surveillance); The Hedonic Calculus; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.
- ch. 18 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Authenticity; Existentialism — Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.
- ch. 19 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault — Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance); Power/Knowledge — Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.
- ch. 21 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Niccolò Machiavelli — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Autonomy of the Will; The Unexamined Life; The Ends Justify the Means — Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.
- ch. 22 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** John Rawls — Justice as Fairness; The Ethics of Care — Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.
- ch. 24 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Karl Marx — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; The Ethics of Ambiguity; The Meaning of Life — Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.
- ch. 25 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.
- ch. 27 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Embodiment (the lived body) — Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.
- ch. 28 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Susan Wolf — Meaning in Life; Dharma; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.
- ch. 30 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Elsby and Luzecky use Nicomachean Ethics VIII to sort Litchfield's bonds: Red's kitchen empire runs on friendships of utility that dissolve when her pipeline closes, race pre-assigns everyone's default friends, and Vee, who sleeps with RJ before having him killed, is incapable of friendship in any sense. The chapter locates genuine Aristotelian friendship only in Red's concern that Nicky stay off heroin (wishing her good for her own sake) and reads Red's sparing of Vee, held by a plastic bag, as respect without care, the recognition of a kindred quality that distinguishes Red from her evil counterpart.
- ch. 31 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" **·** Ethical Egoism — Greene reconstructs the Prisoner's Dilemma with Pennsatucky and Vee in separate interrogation rooms, then maps a variant onto 'Thirsty Bird': whatever Alex does, Piper is better off testifying against Kubra, yet mutual silence was the group-rational outcome the two pact on the van ride. Alex defects anyway, leaving Piper with perjury and no leniency, and Greene argues Piper should have done the 'rational' thing, since Balik's revenge is only a threat while extra time in Litchfield is a certain harm and Alex has always been willing to screw her. The episode shows why honor among the self-interested fails without trust.
- ch. 32 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' appendix, 'Sugar and Spice and Some Things Not So Nice!,' argues that part of the show's success is our cultural obsession with women-in-prison stories, from the film Caged to tabloid celebrity mugshots. It then catalogues famous imprisoned women from history and today: Marie Antoinette and Eleanor of Aquitaine under house arrest, Elizabeth Bathory and Joan of Arc in castle towers, the Salem witches, Patty Hearst, Billie Holiday and Martha Stewart at Alderson, Pussy Riot in Russian penal colonies, Aileen Wuornos, and the Tower of London's Anne Boleyn and Anne Askew. The survey supplies the real history behind the women-in-prison genre that Litchfield reworks, with no single philosopher or theory applied.
- ch. 33 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Praise" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Through a Screen Darkly" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Chapter 01 - Hollywood Doesn’t Know Dick" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.
- ch. 8 "We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.
- ch. 9 "Free Will at the Box Office" **·** Free Will vs Determinism — Mills contrasts Dick's 'The Minority Report', where Anderton knowingly kills Kaplan exactly as the final Precog prediction foretold and accepts exile contentedly, with Spielberg's film in which Agatha insists 'You still have a choice' and Crow is spared. He pairs 'Adjustment Team', where Ed Fletcher grovels and accepts the adjustments as for the greater good, with The Adjustment Bureau, where Damon's love teaches the Chairman a lesson and wins the couple their freedom. In both cases the story doubts free will while the movie insists the hero's choice secures human dignity, which Mills attributes to the Dickian worldview being box-office poison rather than to mere economics.
- ch. 10 "Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will" **·** David Hume — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism — Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.
- ch. 11 "Skepticism for Fun and Profit" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.
- ch. 12 "What’s So Bad about Determinism" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "What’s So Bad about Skepticism" **·** Sextus Empiricus, Nagarjuna — Pyrrhonian Skepticism (suspension of judgment); Philosophical Skepticism — Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.
- ch. 14 "A Happy Ending" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Chapter 02 - A Quintessence of Dust" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes — Barham breaks down 'what is a replicant' into Aristotle's four causes: efficiently engineered by Tyrell technicians, materially biomechanical, formally modeled on humans, and finally intended for slave labor. Humans can answer the first three causes too, but our final cause, our point or purpose, has no ready answer, and that missing fourth cause is the central theme shared by Blade Runner and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? as Deckard grapples with his conscience over 'retiring' replicants.
- ch. 16 "Show Me What You’re Made Of" **·** Aristotle — The Four Causes — The chapter runs Blade Runner's replicants through Aristotle's list-style test of essences and rejects each candidate: rationality falls when Roy checkmates his own designer at chess and mocks Deckard's panic, agency falls because the replicants set their own agenda by rebelling, and morality falls by reductio, since if morality defined humanity then Deckard's 'retirements' would unmake his, as Roy's jeer 'Aren't you the good man?' underscores. Even love is withheld as sufficient, from Gaff's 'It's too bad she won't live, but then again, who does?' to the distracting detail of Pris's tongue retracting after Roy kisses her corpse.
- ch. 17 "Have You Ever Retired a Human by Mistake" *(no index entry yet)* — The chapter argues that once Blade Runner has eliminated each candidate essence, 'human' must be treated as an irreducible concept, drawing on Raimond Gaita's example of the racist woman M, who grants Vietnamese people every capacity on the philosopher's list yet remains a racist, and on Simone Weil's claim that every human being is owed obligation simply as a human being. It applies this to Do Androids Dream: Isidore's boss sees past 'chickenhead' prejudice, and Deckard cuts his secretary off before she can label the retired replicants, admitting 'So much for the distinction between authentic living humans and android constructs.' The chapter closes by handing the irreducible concept over to phenomenology and existentialism as methods better suited than necessary-and-sufficient conditions.
- ch. 18 "The Lung-less, All-Penetrating Masterful World-Silence" **·** Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Question Concerning Technology; The Absurd — The section reads Do Androids Dream through Heidegger's 'The Question Concerning Technology': mood organs, empathy boxes, Buster Friendly and catalog-bought animals alienate humans from the world, each other and themselves until only the 'silence of the world' remains, which Isidore theorizes as the inevitable kipple-ization of the universe. Byron's 'Darkness' and Nietzsche's parable of the clever beasts frame Deckard's drive into the dead desert after his last retirement, where he confronts a universe of dead stones that perceive and remember nothing.
- ch. 19 "Do You Think Androids Have Souls" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger — The Ghost in the Machine; The Question Concerning Technology — The chapter sets up strong versus weak AI through Rachael's account of the Rosen Association's strategy of iterating models until one is indistinguishable, then brings in Gaita's 'non-speculative conception' of a soul via Wittgenstein's remark that 'My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.' Heidegger's warning that technology tempts us to treat others as mere means is dramatized in Deckard's realization after meeting the predatory bounty hunter Phil Resch that he had been viewing androids, and hence himself, as means; his half-measure of wishing other androids did the retiring shows how far he still has to go.
- ch. 20 "The Cardinal Mystery of Creation" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology; Authenticity — The chapter completes the Heidegger arc: where danger is grows the saving power, so Deckard's first thoughts on finding the toad (U.N. stars and reward money) expose his alienation from any authentic relation to the world, yet he ends 'devoted' to the electric toad because 'The electric things have their lives, too.' Roy Batty's tears-in-rain speech becomes the film's expression of the same saving power: wonder at the mystery of Being is what essentially ensouls humans and replicants alike.
- ch. 21 "Chapter 03 - Dick Doesn’t Do Heroes" *(no index entry yet)* — Weiss and Nicholas center the chapter on Dick's 1977 Metz interview, where he contrasted Flash Gordon and Buck Rogers heroes who 'give all the answers' with his own 'bumbling, coarse, garrulous' protagonists overwhelmed by an inscrutable universe, echoing Faulkner's Nobel speech about man prevailing through compassion, sacrifice and endurance. They argue Hollywood must inflate these ordinary characters into action figures, and that this very distortion clarifies what Dick was doing: spotlighting human weakness and the occasional rise of average Joes above their 'greedy, incompetent, petty selves.'
- ch. 22 "You’ve Been Adjusted" **·** Authenticity — The chapter tracks the Hollywood upgrades: the 'bald and fat and old' administrator of 'The Minority Report' becomes Tom Cruise, the 'miserable little salaried employee' of 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale' becomes Arnold Schwarzenegger, and real-estate clerk Ed becomes Matt Damon running for Congress. It contrasts The Adjustment Bureau's David Norris, whose defiance of the Chairman's Plan is rewarded with the girl, with Ed Fletcher of 'Adjustment Team', who grovels ('don't de-energize me') and is released only because he is too minor to matter. The upshot: Dick wrote about authenticity, not heroes, and the films swap ordinary endurance for larger-than-life agency.
- ch. 23 "We Can Endorse That for You Wholesale" **·** The Question Concerning Technology — The chapter opposes Total Recall, where Quaid switches on the alien reactor in 'unwavering faith' and benevolent technology terraforms Mars into a paradise, to 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale', where Quail surrenders because a brain-implanted security device transmits his every thought and 'anything you think may be held against you.' Citing Dick's line that even the most base human schemes are preferable to the most exalted machine tropisms, it argues the films inscribe a faith in technology that Dick himself never held.
- ch. 24 "Nagging Spouses and Robotic Home-Wreckers" **·** Philosophy of Love — The chapter shows Hollywoodization reaching romance: the film gives us a bachelor Deckard and a shy, rescue-worthy Rachael in a classic love story that ends with the couple fleeing together, while the novel gives Deckard a badgering wife Iran and a Rachael Rosen who is a sociopath seducing him precisely so that killing androids like her becomes impossible. Knight-rescues-damsel becomes nebbish-manipulated-by-a-psychopathic-machine, and the chapter insists this wholesale rewriting of Dick's ideas about love and marriage carries philosophical implications that are easy to miss.
- ch. 25 "Scott versus Linklater" **·** Authenticity — The chapter contrasts the directors, Scott's muscular, sensory-assaulting urban noir versus Linklater's quiet, rotoscoped suburban everyday, and their fidelity to the source: quoting Edelstein, Blade Runner misses the novel's empathy-centered psychological complexity, while A Scanner Darkly foregrounds its author with Dick's face appearing in the scramble suit, the closing Author's Note, and Dick's daughters on a faithfully recreated Orange County set. The evaluative criterion throughout is authenticity to Dick, which Linklater preserves and Scott wildly transforms.
- ch. 26 "Deckard versus Arctor" **·** Objectification; Authenticity — The chapter sets Ford's redemptive Deckard against Keanu Reeves's Bob Arctor, the everyman who spies on himself and disintegrates on Substance D, noting the shared scaffolding (lawman, shadowy supplier Tyrell/New Path, nemesis with doubtful humanity, woman in identity crisis) that only highlights the divergence: Deckard is educated into humanity through Rachael while Arctor is progressively dehumanized, with Donna/Audrey betraying rather than redeeming him. It leans on Dick's 'The Android and the Human' definition of becoming an android as being 'pounded down, manipulated, made into a means without one's knowledge or consent', so that Blade Runner imagines androids becoming human where A Scanner Darkly shows humans becoming androids, with even nature (New Path's corn fields) enlisted in the enslavement.
- ch. 27 "From Hover Cars to Substance D" **·** The Question Concerning Technology; The Panopticon (surveillance) — The chapter contrasts the films' technologies: Blade Runner foregrounds gaudy techno-tropes and a Voight-Kampff machine that discloses the truth about replicants, while A Scanner Darkly dwells on mundane devices, Substance D, surveillance cameras, cell phones and Barris's broken contraptions, that obscure reality and help dissolve Arctor's personality. It reads the latter as Dick's fear of the mechanization of humanity made contemporary, mirroring our own self-documentation on YouTube, Twitter and Facebook, and ending with Bruce, 'a dried husk', in the decoy corn field.
- ch. 28 "Through a Screen, Darkly" **·** Authenticity — The chapter argues A Scanner Darkly is consciously about the media itself: rotoscoping inserts a critical break between viewer and screen, exposing our love of scanning and being scanned, an edge that Hollywood, itself invested in media technology, habitually blunts. Against the blockbuster escape it cites Dick's 'How to Build a Universe that Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later', where ordinary people's heroism lies in quiet refusals ('they cannot be compelled to be what they are not'), and ends with Deckard's 'unnatural self' and Arctor's 'soul sickness', both of whom endure, which is where their and our heroism lies.
- ch. 29 "Chapter 04 - Ewe, Robot" **·** The Turing Test; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Seegert opens with the V-K tortoise scene: Leon knows what a turtle is but cannot feel what it would be like to be one, making empathy the litmus of humanity, even though empathy just is imaginative simulation, so the test ironically demands that humans simulate better than the simulations do. He notes the double irony that replicants show empathy for each other (Roy mourning Pris) while Deckard shoots Zhora in the back without wincing, and that the test's real function is keeping androids enslaveable in an arms race of verisimilitude; the deeper anxiety the chapter sets up is not whether androids can pass for human but whether I might not be human myself.
- ch. 30 "How Animals Make Us Human" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Authenticity — The chapter contrasts the novel, where humanity is secured through empathetic relations with scarce real animals (Deckard hating his electric sheep's 'tyranny' because it does not know he exists), with the film, where photographs do the validating: Rachael's 'Look, it's me with my mother' treats the photo as a self-grounding artifact, which the chapter explains via Baudrillard's precession of simulacra, supplemented by Sontag's point that photos act as surrogate relations documenting the loved one's absence. Deckard's piano covered in old sepia photos then reads as overcompensation: abundant evidence, no current relationships, a hint that he may be an android.
- ch. 31 "Narcissism in a “More Human than Human” World" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter reads Deckard's longing for a real sheep as a need for his own existence to register on another genuine subjectivity, the electric sheep having no 'there there', as fellow bounty hunter Phil Resch's devotion to his squirrel Buffy implicitly concedes. It then deploys McLuhan's 'Narcissus as Narcosis': technologies like androids, the Penfield Mood Organ and the Empathy Box are a hall of mirrors reflecting humanity back at itself, so Mercerism offers virtual others that 'generate the effects of relationship even if they lack its substance.'
- ch. 32 "Empathy in a “More Human than Human” World" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter shows Deckard funding empathy for animals by killing androids, then raises the stakes: since android models keep improving, even close inspection of one's ostensibly 'real' sheep might fail to disclose a clever simulation, which it names as Dick's reconfiguration of the problem of other minds and solipsism. The desert toad, seen 'through Mercer's eyes' and boxed with painstaking care, is revealed by Iran to be electric, so that 'the desert of the real offers safe habitat only for virtual creatures.'
- ch. 33 "The Shock of Being Alive" **·** Martin Heidegger, Jean Baudrillard — The Question Concerning Technology; Deep Ecology; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.
- ch. 34 "The Lives of Electric Others" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Authenticity — The chapter follows Deckard past despair at universal fakery (the toad electric, Mercer a set) to his muted epiphany, 'The electric things have their lives, too', and his 'Mercer isn't fake... unless reality is fake', asking whether this extends his circle of moral concern to electric beings or merely concedes the inescapability of virtuality. It reads the film's origami unicorn and Deckard's willingness to make a life with Rachael as parallel acceptances, ending with Iran ordering 'one pound of artificial flies that really fly around and buzz' for the toad her husband is devoted to.
- ch. 35 "Identity Crises" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "Chapter 05 - Just Who and How Many Do You Think You Are" **·** Personal Identity — Feist opens with Dr. Wigan's autopsy of a man with half a brain and a full mind, moves through the split-brain experiments (the left hand writing 'PIPE' for a concealed pipe as the hemispheres autocomplete each other), and lands on Joseph Bogen's revived thesis that each of us has two minds that merely feel like one. He shows Dick threading Bogen's actual sentences mid-dialogue into A Scanner Darkly so the reader experiences a voice from nowhere, foreshadowing how Arctor's self explodes under the scramble suit, the Fred persona and Substance D into separate persons, Bob and Fred, who end up unsure who, and how many, they are.
- ch. 37 "The User Illusion" **·** René Descartes — Mind–Body Dualism; Personal Identity — The chapter interleaves a doctor's line-card quiz of Fred with Bogen and Wigan's claims that each cerebrum is 'a distinct and perfect whole as an organ of thought' and that our cherished 'inner conviction of Oneness' is mere opinion. Descartes supplies the target: a partless mind known directly and with certainty, external things known only indirectly through possibly misleading ideas, and Dick, we are told, flips this picture so the inside is messy and the outside clear.
- ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" **·** John Locke, David Hume — Personal Identity; Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- ch. 39 "You Don’t Always Get Along" **·** David Hume, Plato — Tripartite Soul; Bundle Theory of Self; Personal Identity — The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.
- ch. 40 "The Outer Workings of the Mind" **·** Immanuel Kant — Transcendental Idealism; Phenomena and Noumena — The chapter has Kant complete the flip of Descartes: we know the self only indirectly and external objects directly, because the mind is a car factory that shapes raw material into everyday experience, so you inspect only the finished products, reverse-engineer the assembly line from them, and the thing in itself stays forever outside knowledge. Rotoscoping becomes the visual correlate: reality is partly constructed by the mind but not totally, and the philosophical task is figuring out which parts of the scene are ours.
- ch. 41 "The Scanner-Self" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Transcendental Idealism — The chapter identifies Kant's deeper, non-experiencing self, the pure organizer of data behind ordinary experience, as 'a Kantian scanner', then maps the police scanners planted in Arctor's house onto Sartre's analysis of the gaze: another's look downgrades you from observing-subject to observed object, and God's all-penetrating stare would strip you of subjectivity and freedom entirely. Arctor's relentless surveillance culminates in Bruce, the identity-less pure watcher, the scanner-self incarnate, with a closing joke that Facebook profiles are how 'we see ourselves through a profile darkly.'
- ch. 42 "The Valuable Self" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; Respect for Persons — The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.
- ch. 43 "Chapter 06 - Will You Survive a Trip to Rekall, Inc" *(front)*
- ch. 44 "Follow the Psyche" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — The chapter assembles Dick's survival-of-the-psyche cases: Agneta Rautavaara kept alive as a brain in a nutrient bath, Professor Thomas's conscious brain piloting a spaceship, the wub transferring into Captain Franco mid-execution, and the Rexorian consciousness in 'Human Is', then grounds the pattern in Locke's prince-and-cobbler and detached-little-finger thought experiments: 'consciousness makes personal identity.' Everything is codified as the Psyche Continuity Rule, to keep track of the person follow the psyche, with brains mattering only as convenient storage vessels.
- ch. 45 "The Perils of Rekall, Inc" **·** Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — The chapter runs through three incompatible backstories for Total Recall's Quaid, Cohaagen's infiltration plot, Hauser's genuine defection and self-erasure, or a Rekall trip gone live, and shows that in all three no single psyche links the life stages, forcing a Body Continuity Rule and then a Combined Rule that follows the psyche when mental life is unified and the body when it is disjointed. Paycheck's Jennings, who starts referring to his earlier self in the third person, exposes the rule's weak joint: deciding when a mental life counts as sufficiently disjointed.
- ch. 46 "Gotta Have Soul" **·** Gottfried Leibniz, Immanuel Kant, John Locke — Personal Identity; Immortality and the Soul — The chapter tests a Soul Continuity Rule: the wub and Hauser survive because their souls do, though Locke himself denies the soul is the person, and Leibniz's King-of-China bargain, become the richest man if you forget everything, shows why, since it would amount to being annihilated while a King of China is created in your place. Kant's case of one mental life relayed across a chain of souls yields just one person, and the rule's practical failure is evidential: nothing could tell one soul with swapped psyches from swapped souls in the same body.
- ch. 47 "Future Selves and Imposters" **·** Personal Identity — The chapter builds a counterexample from Imposter: suppose the same mind-transfer process makes the alien android an imposter in one story but the dying Olham's chosen future self in another, with identical bodily and mental continuity but opposite verdicts, so the Combined Rule fails. Intention cannot rescue the Soul Rule either, since in a government-forced transfer Olham would absurdly have to say 'I am dead over there across the room' if souls simply went where we wanted.
- ch. 48 "Selfless" **·** Personal Identity; Philosophical Skepticism — The chapter concedes that no rule, psyche, body, soul, or combined, accommodates all of Dick's transformations, and refuses to blame Dick for incoherence: his stories force our own conflicting intuitions about wubs, Quaids and downloaded minds into the open. Pessimist, optimist and skeptic each get a verdict, the skeptic's being the chapter's cliffhanger: if we are none of these things, maybe there are no enduring persons at all.
