## Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Men in Bright Tights and Wild Fights, Often at Great Heights, and, of Course," *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction surveys the current resurgence of the superhero: Spider-Man's record-breaking opening weekends, 87,000 fans at the San Diego Comicon, and superhero references running through Seinfeld, Scrubs, rock, and rap. It argues that classic superhero stories, like the works of Plato and Aristotle, are here to stay - enduring modern myths that are wildly fun yet thought-provoking, with Superman and Batman now recognized worldwide as cultural icons.
- ch. 6 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors argue that superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, deserve serious intellectual attention because they dramatize philosophy's deepest questions - ethics, responsibility, justice, personal identity, faith, friendship, and family. They press the point into the near future: genetic engineering and nanotechnology may soon make real the questions comics have long explored, such as whether to genetically supercharge a baby or what to do if you woke up with powers yourself. The volume brings philosophy professors together with comic-book writers and editors to wrestle with these issues.
- ch. 7 "Superheroes and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Part One - The Image of the Superhero" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Chapter 1 - The Real Truth about Superman And the Rest of Us, Too" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Preparation for a Surprise" *(interlude)*
- ch. 11 "The One Question I Could Not Answer" **·** Socrates — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Comic writer Mark Waid, hired by DC editor Dan DiDio to re-imagine Superman in Superman: Birthright, is stumped by the question 'Why does he do what he does?' He argues that post-9/11 kids see the Big Blue Boy Scout as an ultraconservative protector of a corrupt status quo, making him irrelevant to a generation that knows heroes from metal detectors and assassinated visionaries. Invoking Socrates' claim that the genuine search for wisdom begins with admitting we do not know, Waid resolves to unlearn a lifetime of Superman lore, and locates the key to the character's motivation in Kal-El's utter aloneness: he is the sole survivor of Krypton and 'doesn't belong here'.
- ch. 12 "The Need to Belong" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.
- ch. 13 "The Great Paradox" **·** Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.
- ch. 14 "Chapter 2 - Heroes and Superheroes" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Defining a Hero and a Superhero" **·** Virtue Ethics — Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.
- ch. 16 "How to Be a Hero" **·** Plato — Virtue Ethics — Using Superman for All Seasons, the authors argue that Clark's heroic choice required real sacrifice - leaving his family, Smallville, and Lana Lang to serve more people - and that sacrifice and the self-discipline behind it are underappreciated virtues, down payments on great goods attainable no other way, as with Peter Parker and Matt Murdock too. The hero, they say, is a normative concept with a claim on us, and since Plato held that the good is inherently attractive and draws us toward it, well-told superhero stories have genuine moral force, keeping self-discipline, self-sacrifice, and aspiration alive while entertaining us.
- ch. 17 "Fear and the Superhero Stories" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — The authors argue superhero stories speak to our fears twice: first by dramatizing external dangers (mad scientists, terrorists, alien menaces), and second by confronting the subtler fear of what using violence will do to our own souls, since habit and a 'rising threshold' of expectations can make once-unthinkable force come to seem necessary. Superheroes like Batman, Spider-Man, Daredevil, and Superman model the answer: they exercise force within strict limits and draw lines they will not cross, fighting evil without becoming evil, and so show that courage, determination, and character can prevail against adversity.
- ch. 18 "The Example of the Superhero" **·** Seneca — Virtue Ethics — Quoting Seneca's advice to 'choose for yourself a moral hero' as an ethical pattern and to 'live as if he were watching you', the chapter argues that superheroes can function for us exactly as the Stoic recommended: Superman inspires us, Batman keeps us going when the going is tough, Spider-Man teaches that conscience outranks the crowd's voices, and Daredevil shows that limitations need not hold us back. It closes practically: ask 'What would Superman do?' and go do your version of it.
- ch. 19 "Chapter 3 - The Crimson Viper versus the Maniacal Morphing Meme" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "What the Problem Seems to Be" *(interlude)*
- ch. 21 "What the Problem Is" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — In dialogue form, Dennis O'Neil diagnoses the fan's complaint that 'the new Viper sucks' as an attempt to do what Heraclitus said cannot be done - step into the same river twice. He reinforces the point with the I Ching's teaching that things become their opposites (yin into yang, light into darkness) and with Darwin's evolution, arguing that constant change is simply the nature of things, comic-book characters included.
- ch. 22 "The One Constant Is Change" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — O'Neil develops two lenses on why the thirty-year-old Crimson Viper cannot stay the same, the first being Jungian archetypes: superheroes are modern incarnations of ancient figures - Superman is, in Jerry Siegel's own words, 'Samson, Hercules, and all the strong men I ever heard of rolled into one - only more so', the Flash a Mercury, Wonder Woman an Amazon, Thor lifted from Norse myth. Myths always mutated as bards adjusted tales to audience feedback around the campfire (Homer included), and modern media markets merely deliver that feedback faster through sales, ratings, and instant web response, so creators reshape characters quickly.
- ch. 23 "The Scheme of the Meme" **·** Everything Flows / Logos — Defining the meme via the OED and Richard Dawkins - a cultural element spread by imitation that mutates like a gene under selection - O'Neil explains why heroes transform: creators get new ideas, markets demand new stories, authors age, new writers arrive, popularity wanes, or an executive has a brainstorm. The evidence ranges over Superman escalating from leaping tall buildings to near-light speed, Batman morphing from 1930s gentleman crime-fighter to Adam West comedian to dark avenger, radio adding Jimmy Olsen and Kryptonite, the Hulk changing color, and Green Lantern changing identity from Alan Scott to Hal Jordan to Kyle Rayner. Gradual change feels organic; the returning fan simply finds the evolved meme unrecognizable.
- ch. 24 "What We Want and What We Get" **·** Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos — O'Neil concludes that fans want writers to 'preserve a part of their childhood', an impossible wish since new stories must change the meme-archetype and somebody will always be outraged. He adds a second Heraclitean twist: the reader has changed too, so you cannot step into the same river twice for two reasons - the Viper is no longer your Viper, and you are no longer his reader. The essay ends with a cosmic flourish about the Viper joining 'the vast, timeless dance of Being', met by the fan's deflating 'Still sucks.'
- ch. 25 "Chapter 4 - Superhero Revisionism in Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "Crime-Fighters and Vigilantes" **·** John Locke — The Social Contract — Skoble frames costumed crime-fighters as vigilantes by definition and tests them against Locke's argument that civil society requires each of us to give up the private right of vengeance to the state - under which superheroes who go looking for trouble are Paul Kersey of Death Wish with a mask. He then reads Miller's The Dark Knight Returns as the first mainstream examination of vigilantism's moral status: Batman tells a congressional committee 'Sure we're criminals... We have to be criminals', breaks laws that shield real criminals, and faces an arrest warrant, TV pundits, and a satirized psychiatrist blaming him for the Joker's crimes.
- ch. 27 "Truth, Justice, and the American Way" **·** Utilitarianism — Contrasting Miller's two icons, Skoble shows Superman becoming a covert government operative on explicitly utilitarian grounds ('I get to save lives - and the media stays quiet'), while Batman insists a badge or flag is neither necessary nor sufficient for justice: 'the world only makes sense when you force it to'. The complications cut both ways - the Sons of the Batman kill indiscriminately in their hero's name, and Batman first regrets not killing the Joker given the hundreds murdered since. Skoble leaves open who is more honest: the vigilante who owns the trade-off, or critics who deplore the protection they depend on.
- ch. 28 "A Whole New World" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Watchmen forces the rethink wholesale by inventing a world where real people donned masks after Superman's 1938 debut, and its heroes are psychologically troubled - Rorschach, driven by the Kitty Genovese murder's thirty-eight silent witnesses, is ruthless yet sincerely committed to justice. Quoting Nietzsche's 'whoever fights monsters' aphorism, Skoble asks whether Rorschach or Batman became monsters, or whether the rest of us are the guilty bystanders; and since Rorschach shows the 'power' to fight crime is a matter of will and choice, Spider-Man's 'great power comes great responsibility' becomes a responsibility that falls on everyone.
- ch. 29 "Look On My Works, Ye Mighty" **·** Utilitarianism; The Ends Justify the Means — Ozymandias, Watchmen's smartest human vigilante, kills three million New Yorkers with a staged alien attack to avert nuclear war, and Skoble walks through the question the novel forces: can the end justify the means? The heroes' darkest hour is their acquiescence in his scheme - only Rorschach rejects the utilitarian reasoning ('Never compromise... Evil must be punished') and is killed by Dr. Manhattan to keep the secret. Skoble leaves us asking whether Ozymandias is a misunderstood savior or has 'become a monster', and whether our recoil at his act is moral clarity or weakness.
- ch. 30 "Rethinking the Superhero Concept" **·** Existentialism — Skoble widens the question to the concept itself: could anyone be trusted as watchman over the world, or is the savior mindset inherently dangerous for a human being to adopt? He reads the embedded Tale of the Black Freighter as the law of unintended consequences - the castaway's vigilante justice destroys the very people he meant to avenge - warning that any hero's limited perspective and fallible beliefs can doom rogue efforts. Moore's move, he argues, is the classic existentialist one of throwing responsibility for meaning and justice back onto ordinary people: if we did our part, no Ozymandias would ever conclude that drastic salvation was needed.
- ch. 31 "Who Watches the Watchmen" *(no index entry yet)* — Both novels criminalize independent heroes while co-opting Superman and Dr. Manhattan as state operatives, and Skoble takes up Juvenal's 'Who watches the watchmen?' as a live question of political theory: is the public's resentment of heroes fear (the Comedian's view), envy (Superman's diagnosis), or guilt? He ends by asking whether we should fear unlicensed vigilantes like Batman and Rorschach more than government-owned supermen - and suggests Moore and Miller are making us look into the abyss and use it as a mirror.
- ch. 32 "Part Two - The Existential World of the Superhero" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "Chapter 5 - God, the Devil, and Matt Murdock" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "The Man and His Faith" **·** Faith and Reason — Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.
- ch. 35 "Faith and Fear" **·** Faith and Reason — Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.
- ch. 36 "Daredevil’s Faith as a Source of Strength" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Testing whether Daredevil's fearlessness is really the vice of rashness, Morris invokes Aristotle's doctrine that every virtue is a mean between two vices, with courage between cowardice and foolhardiness - but since fear is not the only brake on recklessness, prudence can do that work instead, as when Matt calmly backs down from Iron Man's federal authority in Born Again. He concludes that the religious values Matt absorbed - love of neighbor, respect for truth, concern for justice - supply exactly the guidance prudence needs, making faith a distinct form of spiritual strength.
- ch. 37 "The Catholic in Spandex" **·** Blaise Pascal — Pascal's Wager — Weighing whether Matt Murdock can be a 'good Catholic', Morris catalogs his commandment-keeping and lapses, then argues his real safety net is his mother Maggie's faith: her intercessory prayer over his broken body in Born Again is the force behind his rebirth, on a communitarian view where one person's faith covers another. When Matt's crisis of faith comes in Kevin Smith's Guardian Devil, Maggie's peasant-and-knight fable delivers a version of Pascal's Wager - bet on God, since atheism risks infinite loss for finite gain - and his heart is calmed; Pascal's 'greatness and wretchedness of man' also echoes in Daredevil's own prayer about humanity's 'disparity of magnificence to actions'.
- ch. 38 "The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; The Social Contract — Morris answers his title question 'both': Daredevil refuses to kill even Doctor Octopus ('Then I'd be no better than you'), saves the cancer-stricken Bullseye, and tells Typhoid Mary 'You are who you are because of the choices you make', denying that accidents or heritage define a person. To Detective Manolis he gives a law-and-society argument against private killing - 'The moment one man takes another man's life in his own hands, he is rejecting the law... I'm not God - I'm not the law - and I'm not a murderer' - yet his repeated sparing of Bullseye makes him feel complicit in later murders, the tragic cost of his faith, which he nonetheless concludes is strength rather than weakness.
- ch. 39 "Chapter 6 - The Power and the Glory" *(front)*
- ch. 40 "From Olympus to Galactus" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Taliaferro and Lindahl-Urben open with the Greek lesson of Icarus, destroyed by his intoxicated pursuit of glory, and map it onto the Marvel Universe, where a scientific accident made the Fantastic Four 'use their power to help mankind' while their great foes embody a maniacal pursuit of more. The section sets up the two contrasts to come: Dr. Doom, Reed Richards' megalomaniacal classmate, and Galactus, the planet-devourer 'almost beyond good and evil', with the Silver Surfer as his scout.
- ch. 41 "A Doomed Pursuit of Power and Glory" **·** Stoicism — Doom, declaring 'Power has ever been my God', steals the Silver Surfer's cosmic power, and the authors correct Lord Acton: power itself does not corrupt - only the flawed vessel it is poured into, while the uncorrupted are not destroyed by its loss ('Though bereft of my power - I do not crawl!'). The imprisoned Surfer's tranquil equanimity, they argue, is the voice of a Stoic philosopher, and Marvel shares with the best ancient philosophers a faith in a built-in cosmic justice whereby wrongly gotten power destroys its holder - fulfilled when Galactus strips Doom of what was never his.
- ch. 42 "Galactus The Power and the Glory" **·** Doctrine of Double Effect — Galactus was designed to stand beyond good and evil, yet when the Watcher challenges him he cannot help moralizing, pleading that killing Earth's inhabitants is a merely foreseen and 'regrettable but unavoidable' side effect of his necessary feeding - a move the authors dissect as the same bad rationalization used by greedy executives and corrupt politicians, and one no cosmic being can escape needing. Only when the blind artist Alicia awakens the Surfer's buried compassion, and the Watcher brandishes the Ultimate Nullifier while pleading that humans carry 'the seed of grandeur', does Galactus spare Earth, hailing the 'glint of Glory' in mankind.
- ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" **·** Immanuel Kant, Martin Buber — Humanity as an End in Itself; Kingdom of Ends; Utilitarianism — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- ch. 44 "Chapter 7 - Myth, Morality, and the Women of the X-Men" *(front)*
- ch. 45 "The Demand for Diversity" *(no index entry yet)* — Housel reports film audiences' post-9/11 demand for diverse and female heroes and locates the X-Men - created by Stan Lee in 1963 and almost titled 'The Mutants' - as the comic resource meeting it, richer in strong women than typical superhero teams. She sets up Xavier versus Magneto as mythic duality (good and evil) and introduces Joseph Campbell's three-phase hero cycle of departure, initiation, and return, ending as a 'Master of Two Worlds', as the framework the following sections apply to Storm, Mystique, and Jean Grey.
- ch. 46 "The Perfect Storm" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Storm's journey from being worshipped as a weather goddess in Kenya to joining Xavier's school fits Campbell's heroic cycle, and her bond with the demonic-looking, rosary-carrying Nightcrawler shows strangeness as a bridge to growth - the duality transcended into singularity when she tells him 'I have faith in you'. Housel then grades Storm at Kohlberg's post-conventional level of justice ethics, yet shows her shifting into Gilligan's care ethics when she dashes off to save eight mutant children from a government lab, mastering both 'masculine' justice and 'feminine' care - hence the 'perfect hero'.
- ch. 47 "The Shape-Shifting Mystique" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Mystique, Nightcrawler's abandoned mother, embodies unstable duality - female and male, serpent symbolism, a name rooted in the mystery priesthood - but Housel argues she can never complete the hero cycle because she is a sociopath who abandons her newborn, comas Xavier, impersonates a senator, and joins terrorist attacks. She perverts Kohlberg's rule-governed justice into wicked principles - 'her deeds are rule-governed, but the rules are clearly her own' - and her blanket hatred of humanity ironically betrays the fear and insecurity of a repressed humanity beneath: Storm's perfect anti-hero.
- ch. 48 "Phoenix Rising Jean Grey" **·** Carol Gilligan — The Ethics of Care; Utilitarianism — Jean Grey, the self-doubting original X-Man of the Cyclops-Wolverine love triangle, evolves across the films - the phoenix necklace, growing powers, growing confidence - through all three Kohlberg levels to her self-sacrifice that saves the X-Men at the end of X2. Housel rejects reading that act as utilitarian calculation or as the unbalanced self-sacrifice some feminist readings of care ethics would fault: Jean acts not out of duty but out of love and care, beyond the call of duty - what philosophers call supererogation - becoming a female Christ figure whose phoenix image foreshadows resurrection and Campbell's return as 'Master of the Two Worlds'.
- ch. 49 "X2, Superhero Myth, Philosophy, and the World" *(interlude)*
- ch. 50 "Chapter 8 - Barbara Gordon and Moral Perfectionism" *(front)*
- ch. 51 "From Librarian to Batgirl to Oracle" **·** Plato — South tells Barbara Gordon's two-origin story - librarian turned Batgirl until the Joker's bullet in The Killing Joke, then re-emergent as Oracle, founder of the Birds of Prey - and explains why 'Year One' retellings, which stabilize a character's canon, make such a reading possible. He introduces moral perfectionism as the cluster of themes (the self can become better, exemplars and friends aid the quest, conformity is the danger) found everywhere from Plato's Republic onward wherever narratives trace an individual's moral progress - as Barbara's does.
- ch. 52 "Where I Don’t Want to Be" **·** John Stuart Mill — On Liberty; Utilitarianism — South reads Barbara's 'Where I don't want to be' monologue in Batgirl: Year One through Mill's On Liberty passage on people who ask not 'what do I prefer?' but 'what is usually done by persons of my station?' - the pressure to conform Barbara feels as a librarian with a denied police application and a father's expectations. He then argues neither utilitarianism nor Kantianism can guide such a life, since both exclude the question of what I want and who I am becoming; what Barbara needs - and we need - is to make our desires intelligible to ourselves and bridge the gap between who she is and who she wants to be ('Divine my own future... Not a page from someone else's book').
- ch. 53 "I Can Become Something More" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Reads Batgirl: Year One as a story of moral perfectionism: Barbara Gordon stumbles into the Batgirl role at a costume ball and resolves that she 'can become something more,' needing Batman as an exemplar in the sense of Nietzsche's 'Schopenhauer as Educator' — not a model to copy but someone farther along who acknowledges the legitimacy of her desire for a higher self. Batman's question 'Why do you want to be one of us?' tests her self-knowledge, and her 'Because I can' wins her a chance; his unmasking at his parents' graves is his acknowledgment of her quest. The chapter stresses that an exemplar's path cannot be duplicated: Barbara's higher self must be rooted in her own unique experience and desire.
- ch. 54 "There Is What Could Be" **·** John Stuart Mill — On Liberty — Argues there is no single final 'best self' in the perfectionist quest: after the Joker shoots Barbara, Oracle: Year One has martial-arts teacher Richard Dragon ask 'Who are you?', and she emerges thinking 'I'm me — more me than I have ever been.' Against the conformity John Stuart Mill warned of, the chapter has Barbara leave Dick Grayson because he has 'managed to turn into Bruce' and keeps 'reminding me of what I once was' — the past acting as a retrograde exemplar and a Millian custom that blocks her next, still-unattained higher self.
- ch. 55 "Of Like Minds" *(no index entry yet)* — Concludes the Batgirl study by asking who accompanies Barbara once the exemplar stage is past: friends as equals — Dinah Lance (Black Canary) and Helena Bertinelli (Huntress) — who listen with fresh ears, call her out, and provoke her growth rather than direct her. Barbara's attempt to bench Dinah, and Dinah's response of taking up new training, show friendship as mutual provocation toward a better self, capped by the move to the airborne Aerie One as an image of her 'unattained but attainable self.' Moral perfectionism is offered as a lens through which comics help us calibrate our own progress.
- ch. 56 "Chapter 9 - Batman and Friends Aristotle and the Dark Knight’s Inner Circle" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Opens Matt Morris's chapter by asking whether Batman — more inner-solitary than Spider-Man or Daredevil, whose civilian alter egos enjoy ordinary friendships — could have or be a friend at all. It quotes Ecclesiastes and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics line 'Without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods,' as deployed in Loeb's Hush, to set up the analysis of Batman's inner circle of Robin, Alfred, and the rest.
- ch. 57 "From Aristotle to the Bat-Cave" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Lays out the chapter's analytical tool: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship — utility (mutual practical benefit), pleasure (mutual enjoyment), and complete or virtue friendship between committed, roughly equal good people, 'one soul in two bodies.' Noting that the ancient Greek concept is broader than today's 'friend,' it then turns this threefold taxonomy onto Batman's closest relationships to see whether any rises to the highest form.
- ch. 58 "Batman and Robin" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Applies Aristotle's categories to Batman and Dick Grayson: Robin receives training, gadgets, and a mission (utility) and enjoys the mentorship (pleasure), repaying the huge imbalance with the love and honor Aristotle says the lesser friend owes. Aristotle's claim that the young's pleasure friendships are unstable explains Dick's growth into Nightwing; their later renewed camaraderie as near-equals 'moves in the direction of a complete friendship, but never seems to arrive at quite that high a plateau.'
- ch. 59 "The Bat, Harvey Dent, and Two-Face" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Treats Batman's bond with District Attorney Harvey Dent as a utility friendship built on shared, extralegal zeal for justice — until acid scarring turns Dent into Two-Face. Using Aristotle's rules that a virtue friendship must end with an incurably vicious person but not be cut off rashly, the chapter argues further that even a utility friendship cannot survive one friend's viciousness when the other is virtuous — 'collaboration with corruption corrupts' — so Batman must bury the friendship despite surgery and therapy aimed at restoring the old Dent.
- ch. 60 "The Cop and the Vigilante" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Analyzes Batman and Jim Gordon as Aristotle's friendship of utility: the Bat-Signal and police information serve both men's missions, exactly as Bruce's 'I need an inside man' monologue in Batman: Year One intends. The chapter explains why it never deepens into pleasure — Batman's guardedness about his identity and Gordon's doubts about his unpredictability — and shows its fragility: if Batman ever killed, or Gordon had to arrest him, the reciprocity would end. A rebuffed dinner-party invitation dramatizes that they are colleagues 'ultimately no more.'
- ch. 61 "Batman and Catwoman" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Classifies Batman's attraction to Catwoman as Aristotle's friendship of pleasure: they relish their bat-and-cat chases, she is neither his mentee nor his colleague, and Aristotle's view that romances are pleasure friendships fits what they have. The chapter argues her underlying goodness — she does not kill and often abandons thefts that could harm Batman — explains the attraction and why, after her reform into a neighborhood protector, Batman finally trusted her with his identity as Bruce Wayne.
- ch. 62 "The Butler and the Man of the Manor" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Examines Bruce and Alfred: real mutual utility (Alfred's lifelong service and quasi-parental role against shelter and income), yet Aristotle's requirement of equality blocks complete friendship — Bruce is always the boss and Alfred always the butler, each bound by an overriding sense of mission. The chapter argues any change, Alfred quitting or Bruce dismissing him, would itself be an alienating act of disloyalty, so this closest of relationships is destined never to ascend higher than it stands.
- ch. 63 "The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Argues that Batman himself is chiefly responsible for the elusiveness of complete friendship: the promise to his murdered parents consumes the personal investment such friendship needs, so everyone — Gordon, Dent, the Robins, Batgirl, Alfred — must fit into the mission, as his Hush confession to Catwoman ('I am not very good at this. Having friends.') shows. Aristotle's remark that the good man is a friend to himself lets the chapter cast Bruce and Batman as 'one soul in two personae,' the only virtue friendship left to him. It closes as a cautionary tale: a life of mission can cost the balance — and the friendship — that a good and happy life requires.
- ch. 64 "Chapter 10 - The Fantastic Four as a Family The Strongest Bond of All" **·** Aristotle — Man as Political Animal — Opens Ryall and Tipton's chapter: where most superhero philosophy focuses on the individual choosing to use power for good or evil, Aristotle's insight that we are essentially social creatures directs attention to the philosophically neglected concept of the family. The Fantastic Four are presented as the rare team whose family bonds are as much a part of their story as their adventures.
- ch. 65 "The First Family" *(no index entry yet)* — Contrasts the Fantastic Four's forty years of continuity with teams like the JLA and Teen Titans who proclaim 'they're family' yet inevitably drift apart. The chapter locates the difference in the blood-and-marriage core (Johnny, Sue, Reed) plus Ben Grimm, whose only tie is friendship with Reed — a friendship tested from the start because Reed's hubris caused the accident that disfigured Ben.
- ch. 66 "Forming Family Bonds" **·** Plato, Socrates — Justice in the Republic — Reads the Fantastic Four's origin through Plato and the 1960s space race: Reed's heedless rush to beat the Russians into space embodies Thrasymachus' Republic claim that the drive for power dominates human life, and Sue shames the reluctant Ben into flying the unshielded ship. Socrates' belief that virtue is its own reward frames the cosmic-ray price each pays — powers eerily matching their personalities — until Ben proposes the team mission statement: 'We've gotta use that power to help mankind, right?'
- ch. 67 "A Partnership for Living Well" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Man as Political Animal — The chapter's core argument: Aristotle's Politics defines a city as 'a partnership for living well,' and the family is the most intimate such partnership — the Fantastic Four exemplify it. Ben's loyalty to the friend who disfigured him, serving as Reed's conscience, is explained through all three Aristotelian friendships: utility (the belonging he finds nowhere else, from Avengers stints to wrestling), pleasure (the sibling-style war with Johnny he secretly enjoys), and complete friendship — strongest between Reed and Ben, inseparable from Reed's guilt over the one miracle he cannot perform: restoring his friend's human form.
- ch. 68 "The Family During Turmoil" **·** Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Surveys the team's turmoil — Ben's walkabouts, Johnny's bids for independence, Reed and Sue's marital strife and suburban experiments, Reed's 'for his own good' secrecy about Ben's cure — to argue that members leave and return not from duty but from a mutual affinity: only within the family do they feel complete and develop their potential best. It also honestly flags the family's dysfunction, reading Ben's departures as a child running away from home and his squabbles with Johnny as sibling rivalry for Reed and Sue's parental attention.
- ch. 69 "The Ethos of Teamwork" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Concludes that the Fantastic Four achieve Aristotle's complete friendship and become 'partners for a greater good': unlike Avengers-style teams whose friendships are mainly self-oriented, the Four's bond is unselfish love aiming at the good of the other. The chapter adds that they turn the family's protective instinct outward, so the world's ordinary citizens live like children under their care.
- ch. 70 "Chapter 11 - Comic-Book Wisdom" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens Michael Thau's chapter: at a time when wisdom seems to have vanished from the culture, real wisdom can still be found embodied and enacted in superhero comics. The chapter will show comics both reflecting the general skepticism about wisdom and offering flashes of genuine appreciation of what wisdom is.
- ch. 71 "Where Has All the Wisdom Gone" *(no index entry yet)* — Argues that although 'philosopher' means 'lover of wisdom,' wisdom has all but vanished from everyday talk — surviving mostly as the jab 'wise-guy' — and even from philosophy departments, where colleagues are praised as 'clever' or 'brilliant' but never 'wise.' The chapter proposes tracing wisdom's disappearance through comic books, cultural barometers in which superheroes' stories once gave wisdom a recognized place.
- ch. 72 "The Wisdom of Captain Marvel" **·** Boethius — The Consolation of Philosophy — Shows how natural it was in 1940 to list the wisdom of Solomon first among Captain Marvel's Shazam-granted powers, then examines Geoff Johns' JSA retelling as the modern 'but': Billy Batson's transformation is purely physical, so Solomon's wisdom becomes an external advising voice — a device the chapter compares to the personified Philosophy who visits Boethius in prison. The Stargirl romance dilemma reveals wisdom's advice to break up with Courtney as designed to preserve its own authority — fitting to an admirer of wisdom, yet reading to modern eyes as the self-interested calculation of a skeptical age.
- ch. 73 "Skepticism and Cynicism about Wisdom" *(no index entry yet)* — Contrasts Earth X, where Odin's wisdom is exposed as a fraud — a frail human ruling an alien race under false pretenses — with Johns' Captain Marvel, which is skeptical without full cynicism. The chapter defends wisdom's advice to Billy as genuinely wise: the detached, larger-temporal-perspective counsel characteristic of the wise in both Western and Eastern traditions, while conceding that modern readers, unlike those of 1940, can no longer be sure the larger picture should trump Courtney's tears and Billy's present feelings.
- ch. 74 "What Wisdom Requires" **·** Plato — Theory of Forms; Stoicism — Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.
- ch. 75 "Our Problems with Wisdom" **·** Epicurus, Baruch Spinoza — Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Diagnoses why we distrust wisdom: unlike the Epicureans, who trained themselves to discern real pleasure beyond immediate sensation — as Spider-Man's self-discipline wins pleasures Peter Parker could not otherwise know — we equate happiness with pleasant sensory experience; and unlike our ancestors, who saw the passions as external forces undermining freedom (Spinoza's bondage of the emotions), we follow Freud's steam-engine model in treating emotional expression as the true self. Material abundance now satisfies the small picture, making skepticism about the larger picture feasible — though, with Socrates, the chapter doubts it has made us any happier.
- ch. 76 "Part Three - Superheroes and Moral Duty" *(front)*
- ch. 77 "Chapter 12 - Why Are Superheroes Good Comics and the Ring of Gyges" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens Jeff Brenzel's chapter: despite philosophers' chatter about Nietzsche's superman, brains in vats, and the trans-human future, academic philosophy has ignored superhero comics — to the loss of a self-declared recovering Silver Age Marvel Maniac. He poses the big question that drives the chapter: why would people with such powers keep choosing to do good and fight evil, at great cost to themselves, for so long?
- ch. 78 "Refining the Question" *(no index entry yet)* — Refines the question by discarding the definitional answer: Watchmen's Rorschach (whose problematic vigilante motives are bound up with Batman-style justice) and Dr. Manhattan (whose godlike powers shape an alien, morally distant consciousness), together with the Dark Knight and Kingdom Come portrayals, show that even subversive comics presuppose heroes must choose to be good rather than be good by definition.
- ch. 79 "A Genetic Fallacy and Something Too Simple" *(no index entry yet)* — Disposes of the genetic explanation: the 1954 Comics Code mandated that 'good shall triumph over evil,' but since only a receptive audience kept code-conforming heroes commercially alive, the Code cannot explain why we find super-powered people choosing good plausible and appealing. Stan Lee's reduction of every story to good-guy-vs-bad-guy fights is also too simple — Lee's own humanization of the Fantastic Four and Spider-Man, like Spider-Man 2's near-exclusive focus on Peter's motives, forced the 'extraneous' moral issues to center stage.
- ch. 80 "The Problem with Origins" *(no index entry yet)* — Argues origin stories function as signs or interpretations of character, not explanations: Bruce Wayne's parents, the Kents' Smallville virtues, and Xavier's gathering of the X-Men inspire but do not determine their choices. Lex Luthor's ludicrous 1960 origin — swearing eternal vengeance on Superboy for accidentally causing his hair loss — is so bad an explanation that it exposes how no single event, in comics or in our confessional talk-show narratives of genetic makeup and upbringing, fixes what we choose to become.
- ch. 81 "Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Tripartite Soul; Virtue Ethics (arete); Theory of Forms — The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.
- ch. 82 "Chapter 13 - Why Should Superheroes Be Good Spider-Man, the X-Men, and" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Opens C. Stephen Evans' chapter by retelling the Republic's Ring of Gyges passage (359c-360d) — the shepherd who uses invisibility to seduce the king's wife, murder him, and seize the kingdom — as the archetype against which the question 'Why should superheroes be good?' will be posed through Spider-Man, the X-Men, and Kierkegaard's double danger.
- ch. 83 "Plato and the Question of Why We Should Be Good" **·** Plato, Socrates — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic — Reconstructs Glaucon's challenge from the Republic: with a ring making injustice cost-free, no one would keep hands off others' possessions, and anyone who stayed just would be mocked as 'a great fool' behind our self-protective praise; Socrates must show that the truly just person 'stripped of the seeming' — enduring the lash, the rack, and the cross — lives better than the honored unjust one. The chapter then turns Plato's thought-experiment on comic-book worlds: why should someone with superpowers care about being good?
- ch. 84 "Kierkegaard and the Concept of the “Double Danger”" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Plato, Socrates — Introduces Kierkegaard's Works of Love: called to universal neighbor-love, we face a 'double danger' — first the inner struggle against selfishness and inertia, then, once we make headway, the world's persecution of genuine goodness, as happened to Socrates, Jesus, and (in his lifetime) Martin Luther King. Genuine self-denial means working unselfishly for the good and then 'being abominated almost as a criminal' for it, a theme the chapter finds explored in Busiek and Ross' Marvels — while Superman, with his undoubting character and public acclaim, faces neither danger.
- ch. 85 "Spider-Man’s Struggles" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Plato — Shows Spider-Man living both of Kierkegaard's dangers: the first as his love for Mary Jane collides with his vocation — missing her play in Spider-Man 2, then throwing away the costume — though Peter is tempted to be ordinary, never evil, refuting Glaucon's prediction about the powerful. The second appears in J. Jonah Jameson's newsroom, which spins Spider-Man's good deeds into menace, the discomfort with super-powered goodness Kierkegaard predicted ordinary people would feel.
- ch. 86 "The X-Men and the Double Danger" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Applies the double danger to the X-Men: feared and hated as mutants, with Senator Kelly's registration laws disturbingly recalling Nazi measures against Jews, they are split between Xavier's inclusive peace and Magneto's war on humanity — proof the choice of good is not automatic even for them. Wolverine's growth from rage into Xavier's moral community dramatizes the inner first danger, while their persecution despite unconditional, universal neighbor-love dramatizes the second — including the extra resentment earned by demonstrating their persecutors' irrationality.
- ch. 87 "Why Are the X-Men Good" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Ressentiment; Master and Slave Morality — Systematically rejects candidate explanations of the X-Men's goodness: not self-interested calculation (the world's hostility undercuts it, blunting Magneto's argument), not innate constitution (Magneto chose otherwise, and the Cyclops–Wolverine–Jean Grey triangle shows ordinary desires), not fear of punishment, and not Nietzschean pity or herd resentment — the X-Men are the strong and healthy ones. The chapter's positive account: love of the good is learned through relationships with those who are good to us, from Xavier's loving school that gradually transforms Wolverine and Magneto's Nazi-scarred past to Peter Parker's formative upbringing by Uncle Ben and Aunt May.
- ch. 88 "Finding a Strong Basis for the Good" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Plato — Theory of Forms — Argues that loving role models give a motivation but not yet a reason to be good, available to everyone: Plato grounds goodness in a universe whose deep character is just — a metaphysical vision Augustine and C.S. Lewis found religiously congenial — while Kierkegaard grounds the duty of neighbor-love in our relationship to the God who created us out of nothing for eternal life, whose love shown in Christ lets even the persecuted face the double danger with hope. The chapter ends by noting the puzzling absence of religion from the X-Men's world: were its homo religiosus inhabitants to ask what universe they inhabit, they might find in loving the neighbor their deepest connection to the One who perfectly loves them.
- ch. 89 "Chapter 14 - With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility On the Moral Duties" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens Christopher Robichaud's chapter with the midpoint of Spider-Man 2: Peter quits, crime in New York rises seventy-five percent, and unable to walk down the street without meeting someone who needs Spider-Man, he asks 'What am I supposed to do?' — the normative question of what duties, if any, come with great power.
- ch. 90 "With Great Power Comes—What" **·** Moral Relativism — Turns Uncle Ben's dictum into normative ethics: the question is not how super-powered people do live but how they ought to, whether they have a duty to take up the hero role, and what obligations follow from it. Two 'hobgoblins' — ethical nihilism and ethical relativism — are dismissed as contrary to our ordinary convictions (Mother Teresa's charity objectively good, Hitler's genocide absolutely bad), clearing the ground for utilitarianism.
- ch. 91 "Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls" **·** John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle — Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.
- ch. 92 "Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day" **·** Utilitarianism; Consequentialism — Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.
- ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; Deontology — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- ch. 94 "I Fought the Law and the Law Won" **·** Socrates, Immanuel Kant — Deontology; Utilitarianism — Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.
- ch. 95 "But It’s Just a White Lie!" **·** Immanuel Kant — Deontology; Respect for Persons — Asks whether superheroes may deceive the people they love, testing Kant's absolute duty not to lie against resolvable conflicts of negative duties: Peter may deceive Aunt May only because telling her would seriously harm her. But the chapter rejects the paternalistic silence Clark keeps from Lois and Peter from MJ, arguing that assuming the women cannot keep secrets or would crumble under worry fails to treat them with the respect owed to persons, so superheroes owe their loved ones the truth about who they are.
- ch. 96 "Chapter 15 - Why Be a Superhero Why Be Moral" *(front)*
- ch. 97 "The Problem for Spider-Man" **·** Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Ethical Egoism — Sets up the chapter's question through the Spider-Man film: after the promoter cheats him, Peter lets the armed robber go with the taunt "I missed the part where that's my problem," and the robber's escape gets Uncle Ben killed. The scene turns Uncle Ben's "with great power comes great responsibility" into the classic question "Why be moral?" — why not use superpowers for "great personal satisfaction," an egoist's super life, when no payoff for virtue is guaranteed.
- ch. 98 "Phony Answers" *(no index entry yet)* — Interrogates the tendency to assume the strongest or overriding reasons always favor doing one's moral duty, imagining an all-powerful malevolent deity who eternally torments the virtuous and rewards the wicked to show that moral reasons could fail to be overriding. Whether morality is rational on this score is left as the live question the Spider-Man narrative will be used to answer.
- ch. 99 "Reasons to Be Moral" **·** Plato, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — Tripartite Soul; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Categorical Imperative; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — Extracts two candidate answers from Spider-Man — Reason One, that immorality rebounds on you (Uncle Ben's death), tested and weakened by the Ms. Poore poverty-theft case, and Spider-Man's agonized "Because it is right" to the Green Goblin, the Kant-and-Bradley motive of duty — and finds both insufficient to show morality is rational. It then tests Plato's answer that only the moral have harmony of soul (reason governing appetite and spirit) against Flash Thompson and self-forgiving sinners, and Aristotle's "virtue is its own reward" against the thought experiment of virtuous Arachnid-Girl rotting in prison while the fraudulent Norm Osborne flourishes.
- ch. 100 "In It for the Long Run" **·** Immortality and the Soul; Karma and Rebirth — Adds Reason Five — being moral always pays in the long run, where the long run includes life after death — arguing that a perfectly good and all-powerful God would not set up a moral order that penalizes virtue, so Peter Parker's virtue is guaranteed its reward beyond this life. It notes that Eastern reincarnation-plus-karma makes the same promise (the more virtuous this life, the better the next), and that since Peter, Uncle Ben and Aunt May would never water morality down, the morally serious are pushed toward these metaphysical guarantees.
- ch. 101 "Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures" **·** The Watchmaker Argument (design); Karma and Rebirth — Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.
- ch. 102 "Swinging from One Idea to Another" *(interlude)*
- ch. 103 "Chapter 16 - Superman and Kingdom Come The Surprise of Philosophical Theology" **·** Immortality and the Soul — Opens the philosophical-theology chapter by mapping Superman onto Christ: Kal-El sent by his father Jor-El from dying Krypton in a rocket parallels Jesus sent by the Father to Bethlehem, both alien saviors raised as small-town boys. It announces eschatology — final things, ultimate outcomes, whether the hope for justice is an empty utopian dream — as the lens through which the graphic novel Kingdom Come will be read.
- ch. 104 "The Background of Kingdom Come" *(no index entry yet)* — Explains the Kingdom Come title from the Lord's Prayer and the book's Revelation allusions, then recounts its premise: the retired heroes idle while vicious new "heroes" who "no longer fight for the right" run rampant and Batman rules Gotham by fear. Via Maggin's line "The superhero is Everyman," it turns Superman's despair in the Fortress of Solitude into the reader's own predicament when facing pervasive injustice.
- ch. 105 "Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture" **·** Bertrand Russell — The Meaning of Life; Immortality and the Soul — Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.
- ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" **·** Immanuel Kant, Bertrand Russell — Immortality and the Soul; Faith and Reason — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- ch. 107 "Worldviews, Values, and Superheroes" **·** Socrates, Friedrich Nietzsche — Moral Relativism — Argues that in a naturalist universe of particles and force fields nothing grounds objective good and evil, so a defiant Superman who fights evil just because he wants to prizes sympathy while downplaying truth. Wonder Woman's challenge — "Truth and justice" — raises whether they are in league: Socrates and the classic tradition held truth, beauty and goodness are one, while Nietzsche, godfather of postmodernism, snarls that "Truth is ugly," leaving naturalism a dilemma between believing in ultimate justice or accepting that it is an illusion.
- ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" **·** Immortality and the Soul; Faith and Reason — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" **·** Faith and Reason; Immortality and the Soul — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- ch. 110 "Part Four - Identity and Superhero Metaphysics" *(front)*
- ch. 111 "Chapter 17 - Questions of Identity Is the Hulk the Same Person as Bruce Banner" **·** Personal Identity — Frames the chapter with a San Francisco criminal trial in which Bruce Banner's lawyer argues the Hulk — a large green figure — literally was not the same individual who now stands small and pale before the judge. Ruling requires criteria for "continuity of personal identity over time": what makes you the same person today as ten years ago, applied here to whether Banner should answer for the Hulk's rampage.
- ch. 112 "The Hulk’s Bodily Identity" **·** Personal Identity; Ship of Theseus — Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.
- ch. 113 "The Mental Realm of the Hulk" **·** John Locke, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Applies Locke's memory theory: the shape-shifting Martian Manhunter and the irradiated Fantastic Four stay the same people through mental continuity, and the early comics' Banner-minded Hulk meets Locke's criterion — but the later "Hulk smash!" Hulk, who recognizes Betty Ross yet lacks Banner's memories, fails it. The chapter then breaks the criterion itself with Reid's brave-officer objection (the general both is and is not the flogged boy), Alzheimer's and Doc Ock's amnesia attack on Spider-Man, and the circularity of distinguishing genuine from false memory (the deluded fan who "remembers" starring in Adventures of Superman).
- ch. 114 "A Causal Account of the Hulk’s Identity" **·** Personal Identity; Teleporter Paradox (personal fission) — Proposes that the Hulk is Banner because Banner "Hulks out" — the monster state develops causally from Banner's body and mind through radiation, danger and anger, rather than one person being swapped for another. But a mad scientist's cloning accident that splits Banner into two simultaneous rampaging Hulks breaks the account, since both would be causally derived from Bruce yet could not both be the one person — the fission-style counterexample that afflicts every theory so far.
- ch. 115 "Is There No Way to Tell" **·** Derek Parfit — Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity — Presents Derek Parfit's challenge to the whole enterprise: just as there need be no answer to whether a repaired machine is "the same" machine, Parfit's divided-brain case — each half housed in a new body — suggests a person can "survive as two different people without implying that I am these people," so identity questions may lack answers. Kinghorn resists the leap: difficulty finding the truth does not show there is none.
- ch. 116 "The Hulk’s Relational Identity" **·** Personal Identity — Defends a relational account: a person's identity persists through continuing relationships with others (like a marriage or a corporation), against our post-Enlightenment fixation on private attributes. Objections — severed relationships, the castaway, others' biased projections — are answered by positing a God who relates to every person without distortion and guarantees each identity, and who, since divine power cannot do the logically impossible, could not make Banner identical with two numerically distinct Hulks at once.
- ch. 117 "What Should We Conclude" **·** Personal Identity — Renders the verdict in the Banner trial: Bruce is the Hulk, because their relationships continue — when David Banner phones to say Betty Ross will be eliminated, Bruce forms the protective intention the Hulk then executes by destroying the three mutant poodles, and Betty, David and General Ross all relate to the Hulk as Bruce. Physical, mental and causal indicators are mere cues to the deeper continuity of relationships that constitutes who someone is.
- ch. 118 "Chapter 18 - Identity Crisis Time Travel and Metaphysics in the DC Multiverse" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens with Sherlock Holmes continuity errors — Watson's war wound migrating from shoulder to leg — and Conan Doyle's forced resurrection of Holmes, defining "corrections": later installments that change what is true of earlier ones. Unlike the finished Holmes serial, comics permit genuine correction across different authors, which is the machinery behind the retcons Crisis on Infinite Earths performs.
- ch. 119 "The DC Comics Multiverse" **·** Possible Worlds — Recounts how DC resolved its Silver Age continuity mess: rather than treat Jay Garrick's adventures as a fiction-within-a-fiction, Flash #123 has Barry Allen cross into Earth-2 and meet Garrick — and one cannot meet a merely fictional character — so the multiverse is born. As alternative histories multiplied and heroes routinely world-hopped, the only correction strategy left was postulating yet another world, setting up 1985's Crisis.
- ch. 120 "Crisis on Infinite Earths The Story Unfolds" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Possible Worlds — Summarizes Crisis: Krona's forbidden experiment splits one universe into a multiverse plus an antimatter universe whose Anti-Monitor devours worlds; the Monitor self-sacrifices to pocket five Earths; heroes and villains travel to the dawn of time, where the Spectre's intervention leaves a single positive-matter universe. The aftermath — Superman of Earth-2 mourning a Lois who "never existed," three Supermen on one Earth — sets up the two metaphysical conjectures, time travel and multiverse, to be examined.
- ch. 121 "Time Travel and Wishful Thinking" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Distinguishes changing the past from affecting it: a fan killing Marv Wolfman in 1984 contradicts what happened, while Superboy #85's failed rescue of Lincoln — Superboy immobilized by time-traveling Lex Luthor's red Kryptonite, so Booth shoots on schedule — is coherent because Luthor only "helped make history." Crisis instead rewrites cosmic history wholesale, and Hanley notes the irony that time-travel theorists usually save coherence precisely by postulating multiple timelines: travelers don't change the world, they change worlds.
- ch. 122 "More Things in Heaven and Earth" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Surveys real multiverse arguments: the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds reading of quantum mechanics, fine-tuning explained by every possible initial condition existing somewhere rather than by God, and David Lewis's modal realism, on which every way the world could have been is a causally isolated world — it was possible to write a shorter chapter because in some world Hanley did. Tegmark's physics multiverses round out the menu before the question: does any of this fit Crisis?
- ch. 123 "A Multiversity" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds; The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Rules out Lewis's modal realism for the DC multiverse (DC worlds interact; Lewis's are causally isolated) and standard branching many-worlds too, then proposes "hypertime," a second time dimension that makes sense of a traveler arriving in another timeline's "1984." Since Crisis speaks of the multiverse becoming one "at the dawn of time" — something that cannot happen in plain time or hypertime — Hanley posits a six-dimensional cosmos with "supertime" and superhistories.
- ch. 124 "Does Anything Change, or Not" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Argues the superhistory picture still under-delivers: Joe only exchanges histories rather than making Crisis never exist, and the Anti-Monitor may well live on in the not-quite-native hyperhistory. What Crisis's writers really envisaged — Wonder Woman de-aging out of existence to be reborn with a different life — is "dynamic change," making it so no history contains the event, and that, Hanley says, is incoherent.
- ch. 125 "Identity in Crisis" **·** Personal Identity; Possible Worlds — Poses the persistence problem through Superman-1 and Superman-2: are they strictly identical? Perdurantism — persons as four-dimensional space-time worms made of temporal parts — makes them distinct worms with no parts in common, so Superman meeting his counterpart is no stranger than you meeting a friend; endurantism, with wholly present strict identity, could identify them across timelines but balks at the impossibility of Superman meeting himself.
- ch. 126 "Endurantist Past-Changing" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Personal Identity — Chases the endurantist bullet: if one thing can differ across timelines, one and the same timeline can exist differently in different hyperhistories, letting Joe's murder of Wolfman make 1984 "not the way he remembers it." Yet even this yields only switching, not the dynamic change Crisis dramatizes, so the six-dimensional cosmos stands; Hanley closes with Wolfman's own secret plot device for bringing back the killed Barry Allen Flash.
- ch. 127 "Chapter 19 - What’s Behind the Mask The Secret of Secret Identities" *(no index entry yet)* — Opens with the Lone Ranger, Zorro and the Princess Bride's masked heroes to ask why superheroes wear masks at all — Tom Morris noting the little raccoon masks fool no one at the office. The puzzle of what the point of disguise could be for heroes doing only admired, nonlethal good deeds sets up the more generic phenomenon of dual identity to be analyzed.
- ch. 128 "Dual Identities" **·** Personal Identity — Lists the classic hero/normal identity pairs (Batman/Bruce Wayne, Spider-Man/Peter Parker, plus Woody Allen's joke alias) and separates costume as role-transition — the Fantastic Four's public uniforms, doctors' scrubs, Bob's garage shirt — from costume as tool, Batman's fear-theater aimed at "a superstitious and cowardly lot" and the female heroes' calculated "gawk factor." What most superheroes do is the distinct third thing, masking: personas from the Latin for mask, keeping Peter's Spider-Man and Matt Murdock's Daredevil secret in both directions.
- ch. 129 "Keeping Secrets" **·** Deontology — Takes up the objection that secret identities require the deception superheroes condemn, and answers that skillful deception within a legitimate context — quarterback fakes, a painter's perspective tricks — is acceptable, while even a lie bad in itself can be morally right or obligatory when needed to prevent great harm to the innocent. So Spider-Man's secrecy about being Peter Parker is justified, even praiseworthy, because a slipped secret would hand his enemies leverage over Aunt May and his friends.
- ch. 130 "Superman’s Interesting Motivation" **·** Blaise Pascal — The Meaning of Life — Argues Superman inverts the usual identity rule: Kal-El's powers precede any civilian persona, so Superman is the real identity and Clark Kent the ruse. Drawing on Pascal's point that celebrity otherness is a function of imagination — a movie star at your cafeteria table changes everything — and on Krishna's disguise as Arjuna's chariot driver in the Bhagavad-Gita and Christ's messianic secret, Morris reads Clark Kent not as operational cover but as Superman's quest to live the human condition from within, loved into humanity by the Kents and refusing to be an isolated "Aristotelian God."
- ch. 131 "Switching Identities" **·** Aristotle, Plato, William James, Blaise Pascal — Virtue Ethics (arete); Authenticity; Theory of Forms — Maps Superman and Batman onto Plato and Aristotle — the otherworldly philosopher of the heavenly Good versus the this-worldly master of logic and applicable science — then argues that Bruce Wayne's years of intentional self-transformation may have swapped the mask, making Batman the core identity and Bruce the disguise. With Mark Waid, he sees Superman inwardly embracing his alien otherness as the path of authenticity, both cases yielding a fused "heterosis" of identities; Aristotle, Pascal and William James back the closing lesson that who we are is a matter of what we repeatedly do, so every mask may eventually become the face.

## Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Supervillains and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "The Devils Get Their Due" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Ben Dyer's introduction argues that supervillains have effectively 'won' as comics matured: since the 1970s-80s turn (O'Neil/Adams Green Lantern, Miller's Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen), heroes like Batman, Superman, and Spider-Man acquired broken psychologies while villains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Lex Luthor were humanized until hero and villain barely contrast. Citing Stan Lee's claim that the supervillain is the most important character, Dyer announces the volume's project: to restore that contrast by analyzing the villain's relation to morality and society, asking whether tyranny can serve a good cause, whether an all-powerful being is limitless, whether anyone can truly desire evil, and why good henchmen are so hard to find.
- ch. 7 "4" **·** Plato, Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls, Niccolò Machiavelli, Cicero — Allegory of the Cave; The Banality of Evil; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The State of Nature — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- ch. 8 "8" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, J.L. Mackie, Thomas Aquinas, William of Ockham, Jeremy Bentham — Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Moral Relativism — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- ch. 9 "12" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Philippa Foot, John Stuart Mill, Augustine of Hippo, Jeremy Bentham, Arthur Schopenhauer — The State of Nature; Virtue Ethics (arete); Utilitarianism; Just War Theory — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- ch. 10 "15" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Jean-Paul Sartre, Elizabeth Anscombe — The Absurd; Amor Fati (love of fate); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Existence Precedes Essence — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- ch. 11 "19" **·** Harry Frankfurt, Plutarch, Daniel Dennett, René Descartes, Andy Clark — Compatibilism; Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity; Embodiment (the lived body) — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
