- ch. 186 "“They’re So Ugly It’s Appealing”" **·** The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Gender Performativity — Takes the screaming fan's verdict ("They're so ugly it's appealing") and Ian Stewart's sidelining for looking "like a man" as evidence the Stones deliberately cultivated an androgynous ugliness to violate gendered expectations — "they weren't just a bunch of guys who bent the rules, they were off-sides." The blatant misogyny of the lyrics is read as compensation for that effeminacy among the Dionysian libation bearers in a patriarchal age, keeping the manly men at arm's length — while noting only Brian Jones actually abused women.
- ch. 187 "Pleased to Meet You" **·** The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Feminism — Blames "the Father of All Pissing Contests" — the Cold War — for forcing English boys who love women into songs hostile to them ("Under My Thumb," "Stupid Girl," "Yesterday's Papers"), and argues two theses: the Stones don't hate women, this culture hates women; and the men who call the goddess's servants "fags" are the ones who built and maintain that misogynistic culture. The Dionysian frenzy of the 1960s took a dark turn as 1968's death toll (Vietnam, MLK, RFK) exposed the world the manly men had built: the Beatles quit, "but the Stones looked the demon square in the eye and guessed its name."
- ch. 188 "From Woodstock to Altamont" **·** The Apollonian and the Dionysian — Crowns the Stones' prophetic 1969 tour, ending at Altamont, as "the genuine Dionysian frenzy" that ended the Sixties — Woodstock being merely "a glorious and well-deserved vacation from the bullshit" — and reads Brian Jones's death as his own choosing, empires falling "for about the same reasons." Auxier recalls his father taking him to Gimme Shelter in Memphis, the movie that permanently formed his refusal of the patriarchy, and advises parents to make a friend of Mick Jagger, since "Dionysus will have his day" and will take his accursed share of your kids sooner or later.

## The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am

- ch. 1 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*

- ch. 10 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Viktor Frankl — Existentialism; The Absurd; The Meaning of Life — Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.
- ch. 13 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Sun Tzu, Plato — Strategy Without Conflict; Yin and Yang; The Tao (the Way) — Argues Tony misappropriates Sun Tzu's Art of War: he applies tactical precepts like deception, formlessness and 'Balk the enemy's power' (citing the book in 'He Is Risen' after Melfi's jab in 'Big Girls Don't Cry'), but ignores the philosophical core. The chapter contrasts Sun Tzu's monistic one-world view of yin-yang interdependence, harmony and winning without fighting with the Greek two-world dualism of Plato and with the Christianity that lets Tony tell Melfi 'soldiers don't go to hell' in 'From Where to Eternity'. Tony's sausage panic attacks in 'Fortunate Son' show his failure to see how his crimes ripple through his family, and because he lacks the commander's exemplary character and harmony, Tony is 'just a soldier', not a ruler.
- ch. 15 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus — Tripartite Soul; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Argues ancient ethics explains why Tony, who has 'the world by the balls', still feels like a loser. Plato's Republic diagnoses him as a 'civil war' of unintegrated motivations (loving father and murderer at once, as in 'College'), a condition power over others only worsens; Aristotle teaches that happiness is activity with self-sufficient, integrated desires rather than a list of possessions, and Epicurus's 'sober reasoning' is the therapy Tony never gets. The Hawthorne quotation Tony reads in 'College' and his Gary Cooper ideal from 'The Happy Wanderer' frame the point: Cooper in High Noon is unmesswithable because he does not need vengeance, whereas Tony's compulsive revenge shows the world has the grip on him.
- ch. 16 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus — Ressentiment; Existentialism; The Absurd — Argues the show's underlying moral vision is Nietzschean passive nihilism filtered through film noir. Tony, unlike the active nihilist who converts value-collapse into self-overcoming, sinks into resentment and life-negation: he wants to rip the throat of the 'happy wanderer', therapy never redeems him, and he quits it with 'I'm a fat fucking crook from New Jersey' in 'Calling All Cars'. The chapter traces the noir lineage (Tony watching White Heat, the Godfather references, Bogart imagery at Satriale's) and reads A.J.'s 'D-Girl' existentialism (Camus's The Stranger, 'There is no God') and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' as the family inheritance of meaninglessness and death-dread.
- ch. 17 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli — Virtù and Fortuna; The Ends Justify the Means — Argues Tony is at times a practitioner of The Prince and ignores Machiavelli at his peril. He plays the fox with Junior (the figurehead-boss arrangement of 'Meadowlands', the Augustus 'never ate alone' lesson of 'Pax Soprana') and his virtù makes Richie's coup unsellable, but with Richie he seeks love instead of fear, and with Ralph he violates the advice to abstain from subjects' property and women (taking over Pie-O-My and sleeping with his goomah), which ends in Ralph's murder. Fortune, Machiavelli's river, runs through Chris's double-parked car, Janice shooting Richie, Gigi's death on the pishtoon, and the Season Four economic downturn Tony failed to build dykes against.
- ch. 18 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Augustine of Hippo — Ethical Egoism — Argues that bracketing his crimes, Tony is an 'ethical manager': against Junior's vanity-driven blunders and Christopher's Scarface-style impulsiveness in 'Meadowlands', Tony shows stakeholder judgment - holding the line on business through Annalisa's sexual provocation in the Naples cave ('Commendatori'), defusing war with Carmine over the Esplanade ('Whitecaps'), and following Melfi's Eldercare advice to give Junior 'the illusion of being in control'. The chapter concedes Tony acts within an egoistic horizon of self, family and crew rather than universal principle, but finds real moral self-restraint in him, invoking Augustine's dictum that 'even robbers take care to maintain peace with their comrades' and Tony's own 'I dunno about morals, but I do got rules'.
- ch. 20 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, George Berkeley — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; Moral Relativism — Argues Simple Subjectivism ('right for Tony') fails as a reading of the show because it cannot make sense of genuine moral disagreement - Carmela and Tony's adultery battle in 'Whitecaps', Agent Ciccerone versus Tony on extortion - nor ground outrage at the killings of Pussy and the sobbing Matt Bevilaqua. Humean ethical subjectivism, grounded in a common human nature and the sentiment of sympathy (with Berkeley's pin example to explain vice as perception-dependent), fares better: it lets us condemn Tony while explaining his warped sympathy - grieving Pie-O-My more than his human victims - as the product of a mob upbringing that Melfi's alexithymia diagnosis in 'House Arrest' targets.
- ch. 21 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Henry Sidgwick — Consequentialism — Argues Tony is a good man and a bad man for the same reason: a moral code of partiality toward family, crew and Italian-Americans ('This family comes before everything else' in 'Fortunate Son', avenging Janice, caring for Livia 'because she's my mother'), whereas morality must ultimately be justified from the impartial point of view (Sidgwick's 'point of view of the universe'). Using the drowning case - save Meadow or two strangers - the chapter shows partiality can receive an impartial justification, then applies this to Dr. Melfi's decision to treat Tony, defensible only while harms to others (her patient's suicide when she is driven into hiding) do not outweigh the good of his treatment.
- ch. 22 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Immanuel Kant — The Ethics of Care; Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Feminism — Answers the title with 'fugheddaboutit' - Carmela is no feminist - but argues she reasons as a Gilligan-style care ethicist. Her moral voice evolves from Church-based justice arguments against Angie's divorce ('Commendatori'), through the justice-tradition confrontation with Dr. Krakower's refusal of 'blood money' ('Second Opinion'), to mature care ethics that balances self with others when she throws Tony out after the Svetlana revelation ('Whitecaps'). Using Noddings on reciprocity and 'total engrossment', the chapter reads the marriage's failure as failed caring, and the Furio romance and the Georgetown ricotta-pie intimidation as care reasoning that defies the submissive female stereotype feminists fear care ethics valorizes.
- ch. 23 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — Communitarianism; The Cogito; The Social Contract — Argues Tony's self is communitarian - constituted by his roles as father, husband, don and executioner - against the Liberal metaphysics of individualism descending from Descartes's cogito (Livia's 'in the end you die in your own arms') and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract, with the mob boss miscast as a Hobbesian sovereign ('a supreme commander at the top, not the fuckin' Dave Clark Five'). The Naples trip in 'Commendatori' (Paulie discovering he is not really 'Napoletan''), the Columbus Day violence of 'Christopher', and the endless Godfather and Goodfellas mimicry (Christopher's bakery foot-shooting, Tony's Se7en-like murder of Ralphie) show identity as narrative, performed with and through others, not possessed by an isolated self.
- ch. 24 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Argues the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle - why law-abiding viewers bear a pro-attitude toward Tony while abhorring his real-world counterpart - is genuine, and dismantles three rival explanations: fascination (Richie Aprile is just as oxymoronic yet earns no sympathy), wish fulfillment (Ralph is as incontinent and is hated), and identification (imagining one shares Tony's desires yields absurdities like being jealous of his affair with Valentina). The solution is alliance: within the show's fallen moral world of corrupt cops, blackmailing FBI agents, hypocritical priests and monstrous Livia, Tony is relatively the most moral major character ('I knew his brother; he was worse'), so sympathy for the fictional Tony is consistent with loathing an actual one - and Chase uses our alliance to dramatize the danger of rationalization.
- ch. 26 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Argues against Plato's and Tolstoy's worry that art corrupts by infecting audiences with a character's emotions: The Sopranos does get us to identify with a killer (feeling relief when Tony strangles Febby Petrulio in 'College'), and its serial length, psychological intimacy via Melfi's office, and verisimilitude make Tony unusually attractive. But the show supplies alternative moral centers - Melfi's own therapy, the 'House Arrest' shark-and-alexithymia scene, her restraint after her rape in 'Employee of the Month', the 'Funhouse' graduation-versus-crime montage - that let viewers see Tony from outside, so the series invites a complex, reflective moral response rather than imitation and may even be good for us.
- ch. 27 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Argues Season One is an Aristotelian tragedy: Tony is the 'man in-between' who earns pity and fear, and his tragic flaw is not his sins but his inability to bear his conflicting family roles, manifest in the panic attacks that drive him into therapy. Like Oedipus fleeing Corinth, the cure brings the catastrophe - Livia exposes the therapy to Junior and the hit follows ('Cunnilingus and psychiatry brought us to this') - while the plot maps onto Greek family tragedy, Livia as Medea trying to kill her son and Tony as a failed Orestes. The Green Grove FBI tapes are the recognition scene, the loss of mother and uncle is the reversal, and catharsis is the healthy outward purging of the viewer's own bottled emotion.
- ch. 28 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Applies Austin's speech-act theory (locution, illocution, perlocution; with Strawson's condition that a listener must recognize the speaker's intention) to the show's language. Analyses include Junior's 'high colonic' insult and 'come heavy' threat in 'Meadowlands', Tony's indirect hit order 'you get him under control?' answered by Gigi's 'with extreme fuckin' prejudice', Tony's conferral of the boss title on Junior, the made-man oath and Paulie's verbal transfer of the sports book in 'Fortunate Son', and Livia's deniable illocutions - advising Junior to tax Hesh, and on the FBI tape permitting (perhaps desiring) Tony's murder - which show how a woman with no power to order exercises power through warning, advising and persuading.
- ch. 30 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, Socrates — Argues Tony is 'self-blind': against Descartes's claim of infallible self-access and pursuing Socrates's 'know thyself', and using Shoemaker's term, Tony rationally attends to his own mind and still fails to know it. He denies knowing Pussy is a rat despite all the evidence until the 'Funhouse' dead-fish dream tells him 'You knew'; he cannot say whether he foresaw that his 'friendly' loan to Artie would ruin him ('Everybody Hurts'); and he perceives only love for Livia while rage leaks out ('You fucking bitch, that's my mother' in 'I Dream of Jeannie Cusamano'). These cases - with Christopher's unrecognized desire to get caught and Melfi's unnoticed fear of Tony - support the perceptual inner-sense model of self-knowledge over the constitutive model, since brute error about one's own states is possible.
- ch. 31 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Takes Chase's claim that the show is 'all about people who have made a deal with the Devil' and tours Dante's Inferno to assign Sopranos characters their circles. The goomah arrangement convicts no one of lust because nobody thinks it sinful, but Carmela's knowing complicity ('I have forsaken what is right for what is easy' in 'College') makes her incontinent; the killers fill Circle Seven's boiling blood, with the suicides Vin Makazian and Gloria Trillo among the trees. Fraud is punished below violence, so Silvio the pimp, Janice the lead-cloaked hypocrite, and Hesh the song-thief sink into the Eighth Circle, Melfi faces the false-counselor question via Guido da Montefeltro (absolution does not absolve), Livia and Junior belong in the ninth circle for betraying the heads of the two families, and Tony's 'soldiers don't go to hell' is left for the reader to judge.
- ch. 33 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil; Free Will vs Determinism — Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.
- ch. 34 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now

- ch. 1 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, David Chalmers, Thomas Hobbes — Philosophical Zombies; The State of Nature; Mind–Body Dualism — Editor Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that zombies are worth doing philosophy over: an apocalyptic world without government, law enforcement, or private property raises live questions about how survivors should treat one another, whether life becomes 'nasty, brutish, and short', and whether it is wrong to kill a walker. He frames walkers philosophically through Descartes's mindless human-looking automatons and David Chalmers's P-zombies, creatures functionally like us with no inner life. Morgan keeping photo albums instead of supplies in 'Days Gone Bye' shows that what we leave behind after the apocalypse is how we lived - our philosophy.
- ch. 11 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** David Chalmers, René Descartes, Daniel Dennett, Gilbert Ryle — Philosophical Zombies; Mind–Body Dualism; The Hard Problem of Consciousness; What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Gordon Hawkes uses the P-zombie debate to ask whether there is something in a person no walker can eat. Rick telling Morgan over zombified Duane that 'that's just his body' voices Cartesian dualism, while Dr. Jenner's TS-19 scan - the neocortex 'you part' that never comes back - voices materialism, as does Dr. Stevens's dying claim that he is 'just evolving into a different, worse life form'. The chapter stages Chalmers's zombie argument (a molecule-identical twin with no inner experience) against Dennett's zimbo objection, with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' marking the interaction problem for dualism, and closes on the intuition that no brain scan of Test Subject 19 reveals what the zombie fever feels like.
- ch. 13 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Daniel Dennett — Personal Identity; Philosophical Zombies; The Hard Problem of Consciousness — Greg Littmann asks whether 'you' survive a walker bite, testing bodily identity, behaviorism, and functionalism as theories of personal survival against Jenner's verdict that after death 'everything you ever were... gone'. His centerpiece adapts Daniel Dennett: survivors yoke walkers to plows and tanks, dangle meat to move them between positions labeled 1 and 0, and gradually build a rope-and-corpse computer functionally identical to a human brain - which behaviorism and functionalism must call conscious, yet which we can conceive as utterly dark inside. The lesson is that we cannot know whether any system, walker, animal, or AI, is conscious, so treatment of non-human systems may need to err on the side of caution.
- ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** The Gettier Problem; Reliabilism — Richard Greene asks what, if anything, walkers know. Rick's optimistic feeling that Lori and Carl survived turns out true, yet is not knowledge - true belief is necessary but insufficient, the gap Gettier cases exploit - and since walkers can never weigh evidence or think about their thoughts, only externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge can count them as knowers. Walker behavior defeats Jenner's 'mindless instinct' line: Jenny turning the handle of her old house, the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, a walker smashing the department store window with a rock, and the horde seeing through Rick and Glenn's gut disguise once rain washes the scent away. Zombie knowledge is real but limited to simple things recalled from the person's past, the more complex the task the less likely they know it.
- ch. 15 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas, Boethius, Peter Singer — Respect for Persons; Speciesism; Personal Identity — Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife is still a person, which decides whether shooting her is murder. On the dominant Western view - Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellect, Kantian dignity against Singer's speciesism challenge - walkers lack intelligence and so are not persons, so Morgan should shoot. They then argue walkers are metaphysically impossible beings, square-circles: dead tissue that somehow sees, smells, and runs down prey without functioning organs, energy intake, or the reanimated neocortex that movement and sensation require. Zombies fascinate because they are projections of our fears - dead yet moving, an afterlife of horror - a Hamlet-like caught-between-being-and-nonbeing.
- ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; Autonomy of the Will — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.
- ch. 17 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Nagel — What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Personal Identity — Dave Beisecker amplifies Noel Carroll's paradox of horror: why would anyone enjoy watching, let alone compete for, AMC's 'stagger-on role' as a repulsive walker? Curiosity fails as an answer, since by Nagel's bat argument no amount of staggering around a set tells us what it is like to be a zombie - and since zombification destroys memory, desire, and self-concern, we would not survive it as persons in any interesting sense anyway. His solution is that zombies are the endearing losers and clowns of the undead world: playing one is a way to celebrate our inner awkward nerd and laugh at universal human ineptitude, which is exactly why Kirkman's shambling walkers, unlike fast zombies or glamorous vampires, invite impersonation.
- ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; Labor Theory of Property; The Social Contract; Natural Rights — Jason Walker argues the zombie apocalypse is a Lockean rather than Hobbesian state of nature: rights to life, liberty, and property persist without government. Rick's 'I don't think those rules apply anymore' to Andrea over the mermaid necklace is justified by Locke's spoilage and 'enough and as good' provisos - the owner is almost certainly dead and the necklace would otherwise lie forever wasted - while Morgan's house-squatting, which protects the Thompsons' home, and Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo's nursing-home defenders show self-ownership and norms at work. The counter-cases, Chris's cannibal band ('a man's gotta eat') and the Governor, who treat persons as mere means, live out Hobbes's war of all against all and are destroyed by the Lockean right to punish that victims retain.
- ch. 20 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Feminism; Gender Performativity; Stoicism — Ashley Barkman argues that feminism is unrealistic and inefficient in the apocalypse: citing sex-difference research such as Bandura's Bobo doll experiments, she claims masculine aggression and strength are what leadership requires when authority must be asserted physically, as when Rick pipes Merle and shoves Daryl, or Shane tackles Ed and Jim. The quarry laundry scenes stage the debate - Jacqui's protest at 'all the Hattie McDaniel work' versus Lori's 'this isn't about women's rights... doing what needs to be done' - and Barkman sides with Lori, treating the division of labor as survival logistics under a natural-law premise that it is moral to act according to nature. Andrea the sharpshooter and Michonne the swordswoman show women can excel as heroic exceptions without leading, and the chapter concludes leadership should stay with good men like Rick.
- ch. 21 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler, Richard Rorty — Gender Performativity; Feminism; Heteronormativity — Pye and O'Sullivan use Judith Butler's claim that gender is performative to read the walkers as genderless: they keep the trappings of biological sex but perform no gender, and like drag queens they 'trouble gender' when the little girl walker turns to face Rick. The survivors, by contrast, drag patriarchy along as cultural baggage - Lori telling Carl 'I'm a girl, you talk to him' while Shane teaches frogs, Ed bullying the laundry line, the men confiscating Andrea's gun while Daryl keeps his crossbow - though counter-examples (Andrea and Amy fishing for the camp, Guillermo's camp of caretaking 'vatos' led by a former custodian and a nurse, Rick teaching Andrea the safety) show gender can be learned differently. Invoking Rorty's thought that assumptions become visible only when their contradictories sound plausible, they argue survival itself demands shedding these roles, since the genderless dead threaten everyone equally.
- ch. 22 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Albert Camus, Thomas Nagel — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; Rebellion and Revolt; The Meaning of Life — Rachel Robison-Greene reads the survivors through Camus: walkers are mere digger wasps, living tedious, meaningless loops without the consciousness that would make it agonizing, but the living - Morgan longing for the real Jenny back, Andrea losing Amy - face the absurd confrontation between human longing and an indifferent universe, just like Oran in Camus's The Plague. Of Camus's options, suicide (Jacqui and Dr. Jenner staying in the exploding CDC) and religion ('GOD FORGIVE US' on the farmhouse wall) are escapist, so she offers the absurd hero: Sisyphus with his rock, Rieux with his plague, matched by Rick hunting Atlanta for his family, Merle's self-preservation, and Daryl fighting uphill with an arrow in his side. Against Nagel's ironic alternative, she argues we cheer Rick when he alone will shoot Sophia in Hershel's barn because his subjective commitments stay noble even with no objective meaning behind them.
- ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli — The Ends Justify the Means; The State of Nature — Si Sheppard grades The Walking Dead's three settlements by political Realism: the Governor's Woodbury - cohesive, feared rather than loved, feeding his people arena spectacle to keep them from turning on him - beats Rick's West Central Prison, which never becomes a state at all. Rick lets Tyreese's vigilante murder pass, ruling as a first-among-equals with no institutions, no constitution, and no monopoly of legitimate force in Weber's sense, then covertly guns down Thomas and Dexter while hiding behind his cop credibility - 'it's me or you' reasoning indistinguishable from Shane's. Realism cares about power, not morality, so Rick's flaw is not cruelty but the absence of institution-building: he was never a bad father, just a bad founding father, who only becomes a Realist after Alexandria falls.
- ch. 25 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Authenticity; Existentialism — Kempner reads The Walking Dead through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old value-system gone, survivors who cling to pre-made essence die — Hershel keeps his zombified son locked in the barn awaiting restoration, and Shane tries to steal Rick's old cop-and-husband identity rather than live his own existence. Rick's waking in the hospital is a rebirth: he first exists in the new world, then creates a way of being human, and his relapses into the sheriff uniform nearly get him killed. Carl shooting Shane to save his father completes the family's existential freedom (children are no longer 'innocent'), walkers — without will or choice — are the ultimate inauthentic beings, and the volume's tagline, 'forced to finally start living,' makes the zombie world a sternly optimistic humanist story.
- ch. 26 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus, Theodor Adorno — Bad Faith; Authenticity; The Absurd; The Look (hell is other people) — Round argues the real horror of The Walking Dead is humanity itself, read through existentialism: walkers cannot choose, so the humans who attack, torture, and steal from each other are the true 'zombie Other.' She traces Rick's self-made, revisable moral code — from law-enforcer to 'You kill? You die' to killing Dexter — as authentic situation-based morality, paralleled with Kierkegaard's Abraham and with Abraham Ford's confession 'I did what I wanted to do' set against Eugene's bad-faith 'I did what I had to do.' Suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol embody existential angst before an absurd world, the Governor's Woodbury is an Adorno-style inauthentic hierarchy that manipulates its people, and Rick's 'WE ARE THE WALKING DEAD!' speech uses facticity to insist the group admit what they have already become.
- ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; Faith and Reason; Virtue Ethics (arete); Free Will vs Determinism — Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.
- ch. 28 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Peter Singer, Immanuel Kant, Aldo Leopold, Arne Naess — Anthropocentrism; Animal Liberation; The Land Ethic; Deep Ecology — Hinzmann and Arp ask whether zombies can be morally harmed: Jenner's fMRI in 'TS-19' shows only the brain stem reactivates, leaving walkers with a merely shark-like 'perceptual mind.' Against anthropocentric theories, under which Michonne may keep her chained pet walkers as guard-dog tools, they set Singer's utilitarian expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, each of which could support a 'PETZ' zombie preserve. Hershel's barn of 'sick people' and Shane's massacre of it in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' show how fragile such preservation is, while the Governor's death-match arena ringed with chained zombies and his kept zombie daughter illustrate Kant's point that cruelty toward mere animals corrodes the humanity of the cruel person himself.
- ch. 30 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, Tom Regan — The Hedonic Calculus; The Golden Rule — Allaire argues walkers have no moral value and can be killed without remorse: a Bentham-style act-utilitarian tally favors killing any walker, and, following Kant, genetic humanity is neither necessary nor sufficient for membership in the moral community. Applying Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, he shows walkers lack pain response (Hannah's severed half still dragging itself at Rick), language, planning (Glenn's gun-bag mission versus aimless shuffling), and self-reflection, so as beings incapable of duty they can have no rights. Morgan's inability to shoot his walker-wife and Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' illustrate Kant's 'duality of the human situation' — we irrationally project personhood onto former people — and our hesitation is precisely the walkers' greatest advantage.
- ch. 31 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, Laozi — Natural Law; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics — Barkman takes Andrea's mermaid-necklace question ('I don't think those rules apply any more') as a test of natural law: self-evident principles — general beneficence (Glenn's 'shit creek' rescue, Morgan's warning that it 'takes away a piece of your soul'), special beneficence toward family (Lori's 'Don't be so trusting,' Morales's 'best for my family'), and piety (Guillermo staying with the abandoned elders) — still bind after the state's collapse, while 'do not steal' is merely derived, so the unowned necklace is fair game and Rick could take some but not most of Andrea's food. Aristotle's practical wisdom resolves the cannibal hunters' collision between preserving their lives and not killing innocents — starving is the morally preferable choice — since virtue weighs principles 'all things considered.' Against Carol's 'we can make new rules' relativism the natural law outlives governments, and Father Gabriel errs by calling walkers 'abominations,' conflating bad (dysfunctional) with evil (willful) — whereas the Governor, who knowingly ignores the moral law, reduces himself to walker level.
- ch. 32 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Aristotle — Master and Slave Morality; Theory of Forms; Will to Power; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Rard tests whether objective morality survives the apocalypse by running four theories against Season Two: Plato's Forms explain universal truths about walkers ('walkers survive so long as their brains are relatively undamaged') but cannot handle white lies or changed circumstances, and Aristotle's virtue ethics reads Rick's rush from the shot Carl as rashness and Shane's supply run as courage, yet virtues prove relative and luck-dependent in a collapsed world. Natural law founders on clashing intuitions — Merle's racism and Hershel's barn of walkers each claim self-evidence. The chapter's center is Nietzschean: Hershel's barn is slave morality that pities the 'sick,' Maggie breaks from it, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and opening of the barn enact a will-to-power master morality without joy, while Rick alone moves toward amor fati — embracing the world as it is, refusing guilt over Lori's affair, and insisting the baby be born into the Walk Age.
- ch. 33 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Albert Camus — The State of Nature; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid); The Absurd; The Meaning of Life — Moosa uses the apocalypse as a moral laboratory: since 'murder' is by definition wrongful killing, Carl's shooting of Shane must be judged by his reasoning (saving his father), and Hobbes's state of nature — 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — fits Kirkman's world, yet the survivors import morality into it, as when parents mercy-kill their children just as one would turn up a dying child's morphine. Taking up Camus's claim that suicide is the one truly serious philosophical problem, he argues our world is nearly as bad as the zombie landscape, so consistency commits comfortable readers to the same duty of aid (helping sufferers rather than opting out) that justifies the survivors' fighting on. Finally he argues procreation is the worst thing survivors can do — nonexistent children cannot suffer, so Lori's pregnancy and Glenn and Maggie's crib plans are immoral, and adopting existing children as Andrea and Dale did is the consistent course, an obligation that transfers to our world right now.
- ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Utilitarianism; The Categorical Imperative; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'
- ch. 35 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 36 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

- ch. 1 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — The Unexamined Life; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Prof Joe's introduction casts The Wire, like Socrates, as a gadfly that refuses to let any viewer rest comfortably: tough-on-crime conservatives, Hamsterdam-friendly libertarians, hopeful liberals watching Royce and Carcetti, techno-optimists watching Freamon's wire, and capitalists watching the docks and the Baltimore Sun all get their beliefs challenged with no easy answers. It retells Socrates's refusal to escape Athens as valuing the quality of life over its quantity, and sets that against the Puritan work-ethic myth that blames the corner boys and fiends for their own fate while Aristotle's flourishing is rebranded as the American pursuit of happiness. The essay closes by previewing the book's six 'Cases' (the Game, tactics, Omar, boundaries, tragedy, sentencing) around Socrates's own question: how ought we to live?
- ch. 10 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault, Albert Camus — Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Absurd — Crosby takes Bunk's 'misdemeanor homicide' exchange about Marlo as the show's thesis that post-industrial capitalism makes human lives worth less, season by season devaluing beat cops, longshoremen, would-be reformers, the schoolkids of Season Four, and finally the journalists meant to sound the alarm. She deploys Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how institutions train docile participants and then require their regular sacrifice to keep operating, so that Simon's 'indifferent gods' of Greek tragedy are now postmodern institutions whose lightning bolts hit everyone in the 'hood. She ends with Camus's Sisyphus: Simon's call to commit to a righteous cause you probably will not win is the only response that offers human dignity, because 'this ain't Aruba... this America, man.'
- ch. 12 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Heraclitus, Albert Camus — Everything Flows / Logos; Rebellion and Revolt — Fagan traces the show's ubiquitous 'Game' to Heraclitus's fragment of Aion as a child moving game-pieces: the drug trade, police, docks, schools, and newsroom all have rules, fixed roles (D'Angelo's chess lecture where pawns get capped quick), winning reduced to stats, strife as justice, and cyclical recurrence with 'new dancers, new faces around the throne.' Bodie's dying rant that the game is rigged, the failed escapes of Wallace, D'Angelo, and Stringer's 'games beyond the game,' and even Omar's fatal loyalty to Butchie show that neither rule-following nor Omar-style code-breaking gets a piece off the board. Against critics who call the show nihilistic, he argues it rejects the Heraclitean picture through Camus's rebellion: Colvin, Bubbles, and Cutty fashion dignity by resisting the Game even though rebellion almost certainly fails.
- ch. 13 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Thomas Hobbes — The State of Nature; Natural Rights — Allen asks how a virtual war zone can exist inside the United States, starting from Hobbes: Marlo's cool killing of the security guard who just wants to be recognized as a man looks like the rights-free state of nature where 'nothing can be unjust.' But he argues Locke's sharper distinction fits better - the underclass are nominal citizens whose rights to life, policing, and education exist on paper while their substance is denied, which for Locke places an oppressed minority in a state of war within a state, and makes the drug game a rational choice for Michael, Dukie, and Randy. Marlo's 'you want it to be one way, but it's the other way' names that collapsed protection, and the chapter ends with Locke's warning that majority apathy lets oppression persist, reading The Wire as protest art meant to move viewers to political action.
- ch. 14 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Plato, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham, Peter Singer — Utilitarianism; Justice in the Republic; Virtue Ethics — Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.
- ch. 16 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics — McAleer ranks three Season-long deceptions - Sobotka's smuggling least wrong, McNulty's fake serial killer worse, Templeton's fabricated Sun stories worst - and argues that only the agents' motives and character explain the degrees of wrongness, against Mill's claim that motive has nothing to do with an action's morality and Kant's distinction between acting in accordance with and from duty. Aristotle's virtue ethics and his difference between practical wisdom and mere cleverness vindicate these verdicts: Sobotka lies to save a dying union, McNulty's cleverness is corrupted by his need to be the smartest boy in the room while Lester's additions lack all wisdom, and Templeton lies from naked careerism with no redemption arc. The chapter closes with the 'Haynes Principle' - 'you need a lot of context to seriously examine anything' - as the case for a messier, character-based moral philosophy.
- ch. 17 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Justice in the Republic — Grinnell reads Rawls's dotted case lists, Marimow's rip-and-run, Burrell's 'dope on the table,' and Prez being told he teaches the test rather than math as Aristotle's function argument gone wrong: professionals who reduce their purpose to stats and pleasing bosses are 'doing well' instead of 'doing good,' which is just what Plato says badly governed cities reward with honor. The characters who grasp their real function - Daniels refusing cheap felony stats, Bunk refusing to turn cases black without the true murderer, Freamon hunting bodies in vacants despite Landsman's fury - defy the Game at career cost, while Colvin's Hamsterdam and McNulty's fake killer show the opposite failure of zealous judgment without humility or rule of law. The chapter ends on the paradox that trusting professional judgment risks messes, but defining professions by numbers eliminates excellence altogether.
- ch. 18 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Thompson reads the desk-pushing gag as the show's theory of bureaucracy (rule by bureau), arguing along Weberian lines that formal rules, hierarchy, and quantification are the hallmark of all modern institutions - the Barksdale crew's 'don't talk in the car' and Robert's Rules of Order included - and that credit flows up while shit rolls downhill, making people interchangeable and disposable 'human resources.' Cases like Kima's shooting triggering politically motivated 'dope on the table' raids, the fourteen dead women fought over as clearance-rate liabilities, and D'Angelo's Chicken McNugget lecture show institutions betraying their missions, yet the chapter insists the response is not cynicism but 'giving a fuck when it ain't your turn': Daniels refusing to juke stats, Carver learning 'it all matters,' Gus spiking Templeton's story, and McNulty finally drawing a line he won't cross. (Its explicit framework is Max Weber's bureaucracy thesis, missing from the taxonomy - see holes.)
- ch. 19 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Derek Parfit, David Lewis — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism — Fallis tests Kant's claim that a universal 'lie whenever it is to your advantage' would necessarily destroy itself, and David Lewis's stricter thesis that communication requires mostly truth-tellers, against a West Baltimore where Avon, Omar, the cops, the lawyers, and Templeton all lie constantly. Parfit's rejoinder - that as long as some people sometimes tell the truth, deception stays possible - explains how Bubbles's lies keep working, while the heroin market shows Kant's mechanism at full scale: Stringer cutting product and rebranding 'pandemic' until 'every dope fiend in the city knows that Avon been putting out piss, calling it shit' and Westside dope collapses. Since Gant's and Greggs's costly truths still anchor the practice, the chapter concludes The Wire cannot quite refute Kant: it is not possible for nobody to walk the straight and narrow track.
- ch. 20 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Master and Slave Morality; Will to Power; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Clifton measures Omar against four Nietzschean criteria for the overman: as a free spirit he is 'in the wind, so to speak,' detached from home, money, and eventually even lovers like Brandon and Butchie; as a non-dogmatist about truth he uses it as a tool, lying under oath at Bird's trial yet sparing Brother Mouzone when the lie no longer holds; and as a noble of the Genealogy he is an active hunter who embraces the will to power, telling Wee-Bey 'you come at the king, you best not miss.' But Omar fails the fourth test, value-creation: his code keeps the good/evil scale intact rather than overturning it, so in the Three Metamorphoses he remains the lion who slays 'Thou Shalt' but never becomes the value-creating child. The verdict, in Nietzsche's own phrase, is that Omar is noble but 'human, all too human.'
- ch. 22 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Judith Butler, Socrates, Aristotle — Gender Performativity; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Socratic Method (elenchus) — Fisher argues The Wire makes homosexuality a source of excellence: Omar and Kima blend masculine and feminine traits in something like Butler's gender-performative terms, build Aristotelian friendships of virtue (Kima and Cheryl pushing each other's careers), and can make the sacrifices - solitude, giving up family - that excellence in the drug war demands, while the homophobia of the streets and the precinct forces them to keep proving themselves. Omar's crossword comfort with 'them myths' frames him as a contemporary Socrates: a mentor-lover of boys, accused of amorality by Levy much as Socrates was charged with corrupting Athens's youth, answering with a Socratic reversal ('I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), and dying for his code in the city he would not leave. The chapter reads the show's refusal of coming-out storylines - Rawls's silent gay-bar cameo, Snoop's never-confirmed sexuality - as its most radical statement about sexuality in America.
- ch. 23 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Trerise argues Omar is virtuous in Aristotle's full sense: honest on the stand ('I robs drug dealers... I got the shotgun, you got the briefcase'), courageous, consistent, and generous, with even his vengefulness a mean between extremes given a world where no one else will check Avon or Marlo - unlike Marlo he never guns on citizens and even pays Prop Joe for clock repairs. Virtue theory's attention to context separates his killings of Stinkum, Savino, and Stringer from Marlo's power-consolidating murders and shows him achieving whatever eudaimonia his world allows, though his obsession after Stringer's setup, which got Tosha killed, marks his one real excess. The catch is exemplification - Omar is disturbed that children play at being Omar, and Michael becomes the new him - yet the chapter concludes that some vigilantism is a social necessity on the streets and that Omar's swapped body tag names the injustice done to the street's truly virtuous.
- ch. 24 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 25 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings — The Ethics of Care; Feminism — The Rochas argue that the only two women in the Game, Snoop on the street side and Kima on the police side, embody a 'militant feminism' in the lineage of the Black Panthers' Kathleen Cleaver and the Weather Underground's Bernardine Dohrn: women can excel at anything men can, including violence (Snoop as Marlo's natural soldier, repurposing a Hardware Barn nail gun, wearing womanhood only as a costume), and violence is justified when used for just ends (Kima overcoming fear to police). They then use Gilligan and Noddings's care ethics to explain the finale: Kima's dedication to relationships and care for the overlooked homeless victims lets her discern that McNulty and Freamon's fake-serial-killer scheme is an immoral masculinized rationalization, so she turns in her friends and becomes the show's moral conscience.
- ch. 26 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** W.E.B. Du Bois, Kimberlé Crenshaw — Class Struggle; Intersectionality — Curry refuses to celebrate The Wire, arguing that Simon's class-based realism ('more about class than race') misrepresents Black urban life, and he contrasts it with Black film from New Jack City to Menace II Society where these issues were already explored. Reading scenes like Rawls's 'project nigger' murders no one cares about, Bunk shrugging at Stringer's unsolved killing, and McNulty telling Brianna that nobody will look into D'Angelo's death, he argues the show registers an indifference specific to Black life, not to the poor as such. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois's account of colonialism and the slave trade as the genesis of modern capital ('capital noir') and rejecting the intersectional race-class-gender frame as a 'discursive distraction', he demands a racial realism in Derrick Bell's sense: racism is permanent, the underclass is really an racialized undercaste, and the War on Drugs continues Jim Crow by other means.
- ch. 27 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** John Locke — Consequentialism; The Social Contract; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.
- ch. 28 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — The Dialectic — Gurland-Blaker reads The Wire as Simon intended it, a Greek tragedy with institutions (police, docks, schools, politics, press) in place of the gods. Using Hegel's Aesthetics, he argues art unveils truth in sensuous form and that we identify with Sobotka, Bubbles, and Marlo because their magnified struggles are recognizably our own; dramatic tragedy works by staging collisions between incompatible but equally justified codes, exactly as Antigone's loyalty to divine law against Creon's law of the polis maps onto Avon's street rep, Stringer's business rationality, Marlo's name, and McNulty's vanity, all of which go down together. Stringer is the paradigm: the American Dream destroyed by the very virtues that constituted it ('deserve got nuthin' to do with it'), while the show out-Hegels Hegel by locating the deepest tragedy not in the heroes' deaths but in the restoration of the status quo, where lieutenants become colonels and mayors become governors and nothing changes.
- ch. 30 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Brittingham argues The Wire is a Nietzschean rather than merely Aristotelian tragedy, a wrestling between the Apollonian orientation of order, statistics, and illusion (Rawls's clearance rates, Burrell's bureaucracy, Stringer's business plans) and the Dionysian reveling in the Game's chaos and suffering (Avon accepting that 'you only gotta fuck up once', McNulty's intoxicated self-destruction). Stringer is Nietzsche's 'theoretical man' whose faith that thought can correct existence, embodied in the New Day Co-Op, cannot save him from Omar's 'It ain't about money', while McNulty is the Dionysiac man inside the Apollonian institution until Freamon's 'the job will not save you' forces his resignation. The chapter closes by reading the characters' resigned embrace of their fates as Nietzschean affirmation: since neither the job, intelligence, violence, nor the gods will save you, the only response is to say yes to life anyway.
- ch. 31 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx, G.W.F. Hegel — Class Struggle; Commodity Fetishism; Utopia and Dystopia — Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.
- ch. 32 "The Wire and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Karl Marx, John Dewey — Master–Slave Dialectic; Alienation; Experience and Education; Struggle for Recognition — Vannatta reads Season Four through Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition: Marlo's ultimatum to Bodie, Lex killing Fruit for Patrice, and D'Angelo's chess lesson (the pawn as slave producing for the king) all dramatize the struggle for recognition, while Marx's inversion of Hegel explains the alienation of the dockworkers, McNulty exiled to harbor patrol, and Freamon buried in pawn-shop detail by the chain of master-slave directives from Rawls through Marimow. The heart of the chapter is education: Prezbo's dice-and-card math projects embody Dewey's synthesis of child and curriculum against the 'banking concept' Freire attacked, but 'You don't teach math. You teach the test' shows the institutional logic winning, and Parenti's grant-funded project class with Colvin illustrates Freire's warning that the oppressor's humanitarian false generosity treats the corner kids as objects of study rather than partners in dialogue, leaving even its successes unable to show the kids why corner life is problematic.
- ch. 34 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Virtue Ethics (arete); Cardinal and Theological Virtues — Cooper argues The Wire stages two rival pictures of power: Hobbes's New School, where power is 'present means to some future apparent good', the good is only the apparently good relative to each desire, and honor is reputation indifferent to whether it is earned through love or fear (Clay Davis's graft, Ziggy's leather jacket, Avon displaying Brandon's mutilated body to 'send a message', Marlo spending exorbitant sums and torturing Butchie so his name keeps ringing out), and the Old School of Aristotle and Aquinas, where power is oriented to perfection and objective goods like family, friendship, and truth. Against the fear-based honor of the kingpins he sets McNulty's failed redemption and the successful reforms of Cutty's boxing gym, Walon's sobriety, and Bubs, whose prudence in taking the Sun job, temperance, justice at the Viva House, and fortitude in facing Sherrod's death embody the cardinal virtues, showing that even in the 'dark corner of the American experiment' virtue has the power to move.
- ch. 35 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Eckstrand uses Foucault to explain the show's central pattern that 'our thing is part of the big thing': power is exercised rather than possessed, flowing through networks in every direction, so even pawn Wallace can have kingpins, captains, and prosecutors running around after him, and McNulty's fake serial killer shows how the police-Sun-politics network can be worked from below. The stat game and standardized tests are Foucauldian power/knowledge, producing a truth ('shining up shit and calling it gold') that hides systemic crime and poverty while punishing truth-tellers like Daniels and reformers like Colvin and Freamon, and its three tools of discipline, hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and examination, are visible from Comstat and the project-class window to the grand jury that tames the dockworkers' union. Even reform becomes part of the machine it targets (Templeton's Pulitzer chase), so the best hope is the constant accumulation of small victories by those who keep fighting.
- ch. 36 "The Wire and Philosophy" **·** Cornel West, Mahatma Gandhi, Plato — Civil Disobedience; Ahimsa (nonviolence) — Cherry asks why even law-abiding citizens in The Wire obey the no-snitching code, answering through Cornel West's diagnoses: the police's 'evangelical nihilism' is Thrasymachus's might-makes-right acted out by Herc, Carver, and Prez at the Towers and by Walker breaking Donut's fingers, while the bosses' 'paternalistic nihilism' (Burrell juiking stats for Royce) leaves citizens not merely frightened but healthily hopeless, as Randy's 'You gonna look out for me? You promise?' shows after Herc burns him and the detail vanishes. Drawing on Angela Davis's argument that the criminal justice system inherited slavery's master-slave dynamic through the Black Codes, vagrancy laws, and the drug war, she reframes silence as active rebellion: a Gandhian philosophy of non-co-operation ('Fuck the Police') that withdraws the state's claim to citizens' dependence because witnesses like William Gant and Nakeesha Lyles are left unprotected.
